For anyone who doesn't know, sharks smell the dissolved chemicals in blood, and can tell the difference between human blood and fish blood. In real life human blood does not trigger a feeding frenzy and sharks tend to avoid it if there is also fish blood present. If there is no fish blood, they might investigate the human blood, but more as a curiosity and not as a smack. As he says in the movie, sharks attack humans by mistake, except for bull sharks, they are territorial. Sharks are intelligent creatures, so if you're bleeding in the water, chances are you'll be fine. Stay as calm as you can and let the shark see you, just like she did in the movie.

Even though I was forced to watch the Aang movie straight from streaming, I was still utterly speechless by how brilliantly done this film was, and how it's almost too good to be true to have this exist at all. If there's one big takeaway I received from the movie was to have Aang opposed by a literal member of his own kind. Sure Taga was much older than Aang, literally and figuratively, and was made to be foiled to Aang's airbender philosophy and behavior, but what made this incredible was unlike Ozai or Yak-1, this was the type of villain I imagined would never ever want to fight due to Taga being an air nomad and at that moment the second to last airbender. I've always imagined it being an impossibility for an air nomad, let alone air nomad avatar, to ever face an antagonistic air nomad given their pacifism, spirituality, and overall demure and peaceful way of life. I mean how often has an air nomad or avatar air nomad ever had to confront his, her own brother or sister? Taga became the first airbending antagonist to have always been a part of the air nomads, even if he was a non-bender from the beginning, unlike of course Zaheer who like Taga was a non-bender and gifted airbending through spiritual means, was never a part of the air nomad culture, despite his twisted and disturbing obsession with their philosophies. While Aang was shown to go and attack Taga for hurting his friends, I could tell Aang was reluctant at moments of fighting Taga since he was the first airbender to have laid eyes on in 100 years. Overall, great start and looking forward to more.

Backrooms.transcribe: Given how many endless, empty geometric hallways our main character had to wander through, having Justin Long's character from Barbarian pop up with a tape measure to calculate the square footage would have genuinely made this a five-star masterpiece. Backrooms completely nails the atmosphere in the first half. The grainy, handheld home video-style shots build an insane amount of tension, and making the entire environment harsh and well-lit instead of hiding in the dark is a brilliant way to capture that pure, unsettling liminal space dread. The sound design is heavy and unrelenting, but the editing kills the momentum in the second half. The audio masterfully amps up your anxiety to a 10, but the actual visual reveals completely flatten out and fail to deliver on the build-up. Still, it's a solid watch on a big screen.

Anointing a young, first-time big-screen director as the new filmmaking messiah of his or her particular genre is a risky undertaking, to be sure. Does the fledgling auteur have what it takes to live up to that auspicious title? Is this an ordination that's truly warranted? It's serious business, both for box office tallies and artistically speaking. But does the heir apparent truly possess the skills, talent and vision to achieve success on both fronts? That's something worth considering in light of the debut feature from writer-director Cain Parsons, the force behind this aspiring smart horror release, which is quickly being praised to the hilt and drawing huge numbers in ticket sales. However, I believe that the coronation of this new voice in the genre is far from deserved and entirely premature. While it's true that Parsons has a keen eye for the aesthetic, that's only half the challenge when making a movie in virtually any genre. The other part, a being an effective storyteller, needs work, and a lot of it. Based on a YouTube adaptation of his immensely popular internet TV series The Backrooms, the film follows a troubled and largely unsuccessful seller of cheap furniture, Clark, Chiwetel Ejiofor, who's experiencing difficulties in his personal life and professional calling. His failed marriage and inability to make use of his training as an architect have led him to seek counseling from a high-profile therapist, Dr. Mary Klein, Renata Rainsve. His progress takes a drastic turn, though, when he finds a maze of what appears to be a collection of office suites adjacent to his store's basement, a discovery he makes by somehow walking through one of its walls. The spaces are seemingly devoid of people but haphazardly strewn with various items from his life, including his past. Has he stepped into a corporeal manifestation of his psyche? An alternate reality? Or something else entirely? That's what he hopes to learn with the unexpected help of his skeptical shrink. And what will that be? The film's opening half capably sets the scene, creating a legitimately sinister sense of creepiness. However, about midway into the picture, it becomes repetitive and directionless, as if it's searching for what to do next. That's where this offering goes off the rails, turning inexplicable, underdeveloped and outright goofy at times. The alleged scariness of this would-be psychological thriller vanishes, turning tedious, silly and more laughable than frightening. And a last-ditch effort to take the narrative in a redemptive direction involving a mysterious scientific research organization only muddies the waters further, doing little to salvage what has already fallen apart. Many have likened this release to a video game with a protagonist trying to solve the puzzle of the story. Others have said that it's full of nuanced references to the YouTube series, although that would require an intimate knowledge of the source material to fully appreciate it. And others still have postulated a host of other interpretations, given the inherently vague nature of the finished product. For my money, even though it starts out well, it turns into an incoherent cinematic mess that fails to hold attention and left me sighing a big so what? What became most apparent to me while sitting through this is just how difficult it is to create an engaging smart horror film, a genre I enjoy immensely but has been plagued by more failures than successes, with this one being yet another entry on that list of disappointments. Indeed, don't be too quick to reach for that crown just yet. If the filmmaker hopes to assume that title, he's still got his work cut out for him, beginning with an urgent need to get out of his own backrooms.

New unofficial Christmas movie unlocked. Far more complex than I thought it was going to be, especially considering it was a combination of trauma-based creatures and a touch of sci-fi uncertainty. Overall a good watch, and incredibly impressive from such a young creative mind.

Well, that was interesting. This is a well-made horror drama released by A24 that, to my surprise, nabbed $81 million in its opening weekend. Both Chuitel Ejiofor and Renata Raines give solid performances and while a few moments lost my attention, there are few great scenes particularly towards the end. Don't know where the hype came from but good for this,

Hmm. Perhaps I just wasn't in the mood, but I really didn't get what the fuss was about with this. Clark, Chuitil Egeo for, is a recently divorced man who has big dreams but who is reduced to running and sleeping in his cheap and cheerful Ottoman Empire furniture emporium in small town America. The electrics in his store start playing up and upon investigation he is intrigued by a glimmer of light that appears to be emanating from beneath the basement wall. Investigating, he discovers that there is a mysterious portal into a construction that has something of an Escher drawing straight from the mind of Lewis Carroll to it. He tries to explain this discovery to his skeptical therapist, Renata Rainsf, but she thinks he's lost the plot so he engages the help of two of his employees' cat, Lukita Maxwell, and her boyfriend Bobby, Finn Bennett, to film his next exploration and that's when they discover that all in is not so very friendly. Meantime, his shrink Mary makes a visit to her patient's showroom only to discover the same portal. Is she going to be daft enough to walk through the wall into the unknown? There is some attempt made at the end to tie up the spurious threads but for the most part one found this to be really quite a dull and unmenacing affair that is hand-held filmed in a style of Blair which to try and immerse us in its mystery but that more often than not relies on increasingly hysterical dialogue and a great deal of beige paint to create some sense of menace. Kane Parsons presided over a decent idea for about 20 minutes but thereafter is all just fizzled out into a repetitious short story of a film that I felt was overstretched.

I'll start by saying I'm not a hater, I wanted to enjoy it, I really did. But I think some scriptwriting decisions were made that really hurt the final result. I'll begin with the scene where they discover the backrooms. While the opening scene is interesting, the scene where the protagonist finds them is not. Having a clear exit point significantly reduces the tension for him. He controls the space, he's oriented, and he doesn't seem lost or confused by having to take paths he wouldn't choose if fleeing the creature. He quickly finds his way back. This sequence evokes so little fear that the protagonist even goes back to grab a stool. He's not afraid of the place, he controls it. For the viewer, this provides a certain sense of reassurance, since this is the character we've been following since the beginning of the film, and he's the one we fear or worry about as viewers. Regarding the character's development, it's true he displays a certain amount of resentment and simmering anger toward his ex-wife, but the character ultimately commits actions, decapitating Kat, that are implausible given how his psychology had been established up to that point. He isn't portrayed as aggressive, especially not toward others. I think it would have worked better as an opening film to introduce this place through the eyes of people who had no control over the situation. Perhaps a more slasher-like approach, a group of kids who get lost, become frightened, start fighting amongst themselves, unease and distrust grow, and little by little they are attacked or killed in front of their helpless companions who do everything they can to find a way out. The character introductions are rather slow, and this doesn't significantly change anything as the plot progresses. In addition, they explain the strange creatures before showing the final creature, making it more understandable for the viewer and, at the same time, much less aberrant or terrifying than it could have been. Some things are planted in the film, but I think they're underdeveloped, perhaps in anticipation of a sequel or turning it into a saga. I consider this reasonable given the potential of the original idea, but at the same time, I don't think it's the best introduction for viewers unfamiliar with this universe. That said, I'll add that the version on YouTube seemed a thousand times better, it creates a more disturbing, confusing, and interesting atmosphere than this film. I hope many of you enjoyed it, but for me, it wasn't even half of what I had hoped for. It fell short.

One of the few backrooms adaptations that truly understands what made the original concept so fascinating. It easily stands out as one of the best psychological horror films of the year.

This is genuinely unsettling. It's a lovely premise and it is well executed. It is creepy and unsettling and weird. It's the things you want out of this kind of horror and this movie pulls it off well. The cast is superb, the direction is great, the use of this concept and its associated effects is executed flawlessly. For what this is, it is just great.

Hung well. The epilogue spoils any surprise of what the backrooms is, the therapist-patient thing is kind of naff. It's unclear who the main character is. I think they tied the Clark character too much to the backrooms, where it should have been its own character. Some unsettling moments, but overall the writing let it down. Some nice creppy surreal imagery, but the imposed story of Clark took over. Would have been better as pure horror atmosphere, where the mysteries of the backrooms reveal themselves as the characters travel through them. Clark's family drama just detracted from this. It's a pity, could have been better I'm afraid. The therapist backstory was so unclear what it actually meant. I didn't really care for them.

Score, 3 out of 10, an engaging walk to nowhere I don't like movies that go nowhere, don't make any sense, or lack an actual ending. And backrooms? It's the poster child for all three. I feel like I've wasted a part of my life that I will never get back, time that could have been better spent watching a different movie. The concept is solid. Kane Parsons, the 20-year-old director behind the viral YouTube series, brings the internet's favorite liminal space nightmare to the big screen. Chiwetel Ejiofor plays Clark, a failed architect and struggling furniture store owner who discovers a doorway in his basement to an infinite labyrinth of yellow-walled, fluorescent lit rooms. Renata Rains plays his therapist, Mary, who follows him in. The production design is genuinely impressive the backrooms feel unsettlingly real and deeply disorienting. But that's where the praise ends. Having said that, the movie was engaging and I didn't realize that I didn't like it till the credits rolled, I was invested, the atmosphere is thick, the dread is palpable, and Ejiofor's performance is committed. The first 70 minutes deliver exactly what you'd hope, eerie corridors, unsettling silence, and a creeping sense that reality itself is unraveling. Then the film loses its footing. The momentum shifts, the tension dissipates, and the narrative attempts to add meaning without committing to anything concrete. Clark explains that the backrooms misremembers people, creating imperfect replicas of reality. The monster, revealed as a distorted, pirate-costumed version of Clark himself, kills him in a moment that lands with a dull thud. Mary escapes, or does she? The final shot shows a malformed replica of Mary slumped in an interrogation chair, and that's the kind of ending that thinks it's being clever but is really just being lazy. The film offers no solutions, no rules, no answers, just a mountain of unanswered questions and an audience that stopped caring. I was left with, well, nothing. No resolution, no catharsis, no desire to ever revisit this world. Many viewers share this frustration, audience reviews are split, with some praising the atmosphere and others decrying the hollow, confused ending. It earns its three points for the production values, which ain't half bad. The set design, cinematography, and EgeoForce performance deserve some credit. But the story goes nowhere, the ending is empty, and the experience left me feeling cheated. I could have spent those 105 minutes on something that actually respected my time.

Translating an internet legend to the big screen is a huge challenge, but A24 and director Kane Parsons managed to nail the creepy aesthetic of the famous backrooms. By relying heavily on practical effects rather than just green screens, they made the endless yellow maze feel incredibly real, dirty, and deeply claustrophobic. The visual design is the true star here, perfectly capturing that weird liminal space vibe where everything looks familiar but feels fundamentally wrong. Parsons shows surprising maturity as a young director, using steady camera work and patience to build a genuinely oppressive atmosphere right from the opening scene. The movie's unsettling vibe is heavily boosted by its brilliant sound design and strong lead performances. The constant, annoying hum of the old fluorescent lights slowly chips away at your sanity, and when the movie suddenly shifts to dead silence, the tension becomes almost unbearable. On the acting side, Chiwetel Ejiofor does some heavy lifting acting against basically nothing, using his body language to perfectly portray a man losing his mind in isolation. Renata Rainsve also shines as his therapist, bringing a much-needed touch of humanity and warmth that contrasts beautifully with the cold, lifeless hallways. Unfortunately, the movie stumbles hard when it comes to the script and pacing. Stretching a minimalist concept into a two-hour runtime creates a massive drag in the middle, turning what should be terrifying into something kind of boring and repetitive. The film also falls into the modern trap of trying to force a deep, intellectual metaphor about trauma, which just slows the story down. Worse yet, they decided to actually show the threat, a generic CGI monster that completely ruins the mysterious, existential dread the empty rooms had already built up so well. Because the main character isn't given much of a personality, it eventually becomes hard to stay emotionally invested in his survival. The ending only adds to the frustration, wrapping things up abruptly while clearly planting seeds for future sequels instead of giving us a satisfying, standalone conclusion. It feels a bit like a corporate cash grab trying to turn a weird, anonymous internet mystery into a predictable movie franchise. Still, even with these glaring issues, the jump from YouTube to a Hollywood feature is an impressive technical achievement. It is definitely worth seeing on the biggest screen you can find, just to experience the incredible visuals and sound for yourself, as the sheer dread of those endless yellow rooms might hit you completely differently.

From its trailer, this seemed like a good movie. In watching, though, it was a little disappointing. I don't mind a movie leaving some lingering questions, but I think this one didn't reveal enough. I don't require a neat, fully resolved Hollywood ending, but I need a little more than this movie gave. I had some theories about why things were happening in the movie, then there was a new plot element that may affect that theory. Or not. It's difficult to say, because not enough is revealed. Some movies leave lingering questions and end on cliffhangers to hint at, or even ensure a sequel. However, if the movie doesn't reveal enough, there won't be enough viewer interest to warrant a sequel. Although I would like to see a sequel or a series developed from this, I suspect it won't happen because not enough viewers were satisfied. I also think this is somewhat derivative of the series' severance, and it needs to prove that it needs to exist.

Buddy.transcribe: If you like puppets, practical effects, and grotesque horror that is disguised as something cutesy, then Buddy is a must-see. As a horror film, it's surprising because it feels fresh and original with not only its comedic roots and psychological elements but also because it thrusts the audience into a bloodthirsty wonderland ruled by a demented orange unicorn eager to twist your head off. https://bit.ly slash its buddy

Buddy, 2026, starts like a fake children's show, giving Major Don't Hug Me I'm Scared and Amanda the adventure game vibes, before going off the rails. After showing fake Barney-style episodes, it abruptly shifts to a real-world family. The mom realizes something is wrong after her daughter gets dragged into Buddy's dimension. The mid-movie dimension hopping between mom's real-world investigation and the weird realm felt unnecessary and like a totally different film, but once mom enters Buddy's world, it gets good again. Unique plot for sure. It has solid body horror, though it honestly could've used way more gore for a mascot slasher. The ending is pure gold, a 50-50 mix of wholesome-aw-happy ending, and wow, while that shit sucks for you, face with tears of joy verdict, confusing mid-movie shift aside, Buddy is a hilariously tragic, dark, nostalgic horror trip.

Buddy feels like a deranged children's show discovered on a cursed VHS tape, loud, colorful, impressively handmade, and increasingly hostile to its audience. The puppetry, sets, and practical effects are the main attraction, and Casper Kelly commits so completely to the nightmare logic that even the weaker jokes have a fascinating texture. Unfortunately, what works brilliantly is a sketch strains at feature length. The film keeps escalating without finding enough emotional or comedic variety, so the shock of its premise gradually becomes repetition. Kristen Milioti and the cast sell the panic, while the songs are obnoxiously catchy in exactly the right way. I admired how unapologetically strange it is more than I actually enjoyed it. A memorable orange menace trapped inside a movie that needed a sharper edit, and yes, the end credits song absolutely rules.

Colony.transcribe: Colony is a marginal departure from your classic zombie flick. While intelligently written, there's not a lot on offer here, aside from a zombie hive mind proposition that distinguishes this outbreak zombie horror disaster drama from others in the genre. That's not to say it's not worth a look if you like this kind of thing. The acting is excellent, the characters have a genuine depth, offering up predictably human responses, for better or worse, to the unfolding disaster that befalls them. Action is solid, too, with lots of zombie thrills but little in the way of genuine scares, backed by solid choreography and cinematics. In summary, Colony isn't doing anything overly new, but its script offers enough interest and excitement to make this film a worthwhile watch.

This is another great example of how Koreans understand zombie movies. Just like with Train to Busan this movie does something interesting with the concept rather than just repeat the tropes we have already seen. There is a great deal of urgency in this movie and the actors and directors pull this off very well. The effects are very high class and the overall presentation is highly proficient. I did enjoy this quite a lot and I recommend it to anyone interested in the genre.

Colony is so smart and exhilarating, with breathtaking cinematography by Byun Bang Sun. The fact that an outbreak film is doing something different rather than rehashing everything that came before it is enough to warrant a watch. But it's such a clever spin on the genre, it ends up clawing and biting its way to being one of the best films of the year. https://bit.ly//colony26

I wasn't inspired by the start of this film as it resembled a sort of foaming-at-the-mouth edition of The Kids from Fame, but once it settles down it's actually quite a decent hybrid of a horror movie and a sci-fi thriller. It's following a presentation by a tech CEO, Kim Jong Tae, who is advancing the theories of communal communication and learning, itself quite a terrifying thought, that the disgruntled Soo Young Chil, who he won, decides to seek his revenge on that man whom he accuses of stealing his revolutionary ideas and then firing him. He injects him with a serum that sees a remarkable effect on his Earthswile boss and proves contagious to just about everyone he comes into contact with, with this teeth. This conference is taking place adjacent to a shopping mall so as these now rabid creatures spread that spells trouble for a disparate bunch of shoppers who managed to seek shelter in one of the shops. With the behavior of the Baying humans outside clearly adapting from the more moronic to something altogether more effective, they realize that help is staying firmly on the outside and that they are are going to have to save themselves. Luckily, all of their phones still work and amongst the group is a professor, Se Jong, Jun Ji Hyun, who was at the seminar, so after a remote assessment with her peers, they conclude that they must isolate Soo from his guardians and use him as some sort of vaccine. Easier said than done, but that's their task. You won't often see me review animated films. That's because I remember what cartoons were like when I was growing up as a baby boomer, and I loved them, especially Looney Tunes. In fact, in my view, most of today's headache-inducing animation is overly manic and overly silly, releases that pale in comparison to those classic old-school offerings. For those who agree with me, however, there's a new release out there that serves as a fitting homage to those works of days gone by that pays a fitting tribute to them while simultaneously incorporating fresh, contemporary material that does justice to its source material, Coyote vs Acme. Based on the long-running comical desert conflict between the Roadrunner and the Bird's perpetually unsuccessful nemesis, while Egh Coyote, this feature-length tale brilliantly fuses animation and live action in the same vein as Who Framed Roger Rabbit? 1988, in an inventive new story. When the Coyote realizes that all of his efforts to entrap his target using an assortment of inherently faulty products from the infamous Acme Corporation, he decides to try a new tactic to fulfill his goal, sue Acme in court, with the Roadrunner serving as a first-hand witness to all of the product failures, thereby granting him ready access to the Bird and putting him one step closer to realizing his long-hoped for dinner. He gets the idea after seeing a television commercial for Shady Albuquerque accident attorney Kevin Avery, Will Forte, a lawyer known for bringing and settling many cartoon product injury cases against Acme and its chief legal counsel, and boastful law school rival, Buddy Crane, John Cena. But can Avery at last best his old foe through this lawsuit? What ensues is a smart, insightful corporate satire and lawyer parody in which the two attorneys battle one another surrounded by a host of beloved Warner Brothers cartoon characters presented in ways viewers have never seen them before, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Sylvester, Tweedie, Granny, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn and the Tasmanian Devil, among others. The result is a delightfully humorous tale strategically peppered with memorable Easter eggs from the franchise source material in a present-day narrative that's unquestionably unusual but that never feels forced or implausible, comparatively speaking, that is. Admittedly, the picture isn't reproaringly funny, but it's definitely modestly amusing and successfully avoids the aforementioned pitfalls that weigh down most contemporary animated features. Director Dave Green's third big-screen effort will nostalgically warm the hearts of audiences who grew up with these flawed but familiar characters, evoking moderate chuckles as they're showcased in a largely new light, quite a nifty trick to pull off as successfully as the filmmaker has done here. Yet, if nothing further comes out of this release, though, given its box office success, I doubt that will happen, one likely won't be sorry when it ends, having deservedly earned the celebrated that's all. Folks sign off that viewers have come to associate with this cherished body of work.

The Acme Corporation has finally met an adversary it can't flatten with an anvil, a courtroom, and the result is an unexpectedly charming Looney Tunes comedy in Coyote vs. Acme. The premise is inspired after yet another Acme product goes spectacularly wrong, while E! Coyote takes the company to court with the help of a down-on-his-luck lawyer. It is exactly the kind of ridiculous escalation that feels appropriate for a character who has spent decades ordering increasingly elaborate devices to catch one very fast bird. Better yet, the film actually makes something of the idea, turning Acme's absurd catalogue into the basis for a surprisingly effective corporate satire. Most importantly, the movie feels like Looney Tunes. The slapstick is broad, the visual gags come fast, and the dialogue occasionally has the same mischievous snap as the cartoon's. Not every joke hits its target, but there are enough genuine laughs to keep the comedy firing. The satire is similarly effective, poking fun at corporate indifference and legal maneuvering without becoming so self-important that it forgets this is, fundamentally, a movie about a coyote suing a cartoon company. The live action and animation are also blended impressively well. There are a handful of moments where the scenes show, but for the most part the cartoon characters inhabit the live action world naturally. It helps that the film doesn't treat the Looney Tunes characters as museum pieces. They are allowed to be funny, chaotic and occasionally ridiculous in precisely the way they should be. John Cena is another highlight. As the smug corporate attorney, he plays the increasingly absurd circumstances with such complete seriousness that it becomes a joke in itself. Additionally, there is also more hard in the film than one might expect, giving the story some emotional weight beneath all the courtroom theatrics and exploding ACME merchandise. Unfortunately, the film's biggest strength is also its biggest weakness. The premise is so clever that it creates expectations the movie doesn't entirely satisfy. What could have been a wonderfully strange, unpredictable collision of courtroom comedy and Looney Tunes madness often settles into a fairly conventional underdog legal story. The subplot involving ACME selling its products specifically to cartoon characters feels particularly unnecessary, adding complication without much payoff. The pacing is another problem. Coyote vs ACME isn't exactly slow, but it is uneven. The first half has a lively rhythm and plenty of personality, somewhere around the midpoint, however, the story may start to feel like a bit of a slog. Some of the acting doesn't help either, particularly with Lana Condor as Paige Avery, proving less convincing than the stronger performances around her. The legalese may also make the movie somewhat harder for younger viewers to follow than its Looney Tunes packaging suggests. While Coyote vs ACME is quite entertaining, it feels like it doesn't realize its full potential. The premise promises something wonderfully creative, and the film delivers just enough of that promise to make the missed opportunities frustrating. There is a genuinely funny, affectionate Looney Tunes movie in here, along with a terrific central idea and a welcome amount of heart. It just needed to be a little bolder and more consistent.

Coyote vs Acme is a genuinely fun surprise. The gimmick, while E! Coyote suing Acme Corp for decades of faulty products, staged as a courtroom dramedy, could have been a one-joke premise, but it earns its laughs by taking the legal thriller framing semi-seriously. John Cena is a good sport as the smarmy corporate lawyer, and the blend of live action with classic Looney Tunes-style animation is charming without leaning too hard on nostalgia. It sags a bit in the middle once the courtroom stuff settles into formula, and some jokes land softer the second time around. Still, there's real heart here, and knowing the studio nearly buried this thing for a tax write-off makes rooting for it even easier. Solid family entertainment, not essential, but worth the watch.

Coyote vs Acme finally got released after Warner Bros. tried to shelve the project for a $30 million tax write-off. It is exactly as I expected it to be, funny, action-packed, emotional, and self-aware. The blend of live action and animation is really cool because the real humans use animated props in the same vein as who framed Roger Rabbit, but the reason it feels more believable here is because instead of puppeteering the animated props, the human actors hold stand-ins that get replaced in post-production before release. Yes, I honestly believe actors holding real props and then replacing them in the editing is more believable than puppeteering because how do you puppet an animated prop? Anywho, the characters' roles in the movie, specifically the Looney Tunes characters, felt like an homage to classic crime films, like how Bugs Bunny's role as a whistleblower is similar to Deep Throat from All the President's Men, 1976. While Forte and John Cena's live-action acting was also great, delivering some funny moments together, while Forte also provides some emotional scenes between him and Wally Coyote. My only issue is that Wally Coyote still doesn't talk. This might come as a shocker, but I'm actually getting sick of these types of movies not letting the silent character talk. While Wally Coyote's signs and nude expressions works for a 22-minute cartoon, for a 90-minute movie, dialogue is necessary to ensure proper character interactions. Even in Wally, the title character doesn't entirely not talk. He just talks less. Coyote vs. Acme is still a pure delight despite this, and I really wished Warner Brothers decided to release this any sooner.

Davis, Chris Hemsworth, is one of those rare breeds of thieves. He has scruples about violence and so always wants to avoid hurting those whom he robs. It's a sound policy as usually it is the couriers he is relieving of their diamonds, or watches, or jewels. His latest job didn't quite go to plan though, and feeling a bit unnerved he tells his aging fence money, Nick Nolte, that he wants out. He's not the kind of man to let the job go unfinished, so drafts in his far less scrupulous pal Orman, Barry Keoghan, who is about as subtle as an air raid. When Davis hears of the robbery, he confronts money and that's when the wheels of his well-oiled machine begin to come off as the motorcycling Orman is instructed to turn his attentions on our now disillusioned thief. Meantime, insurance underwriter Sharon, Halle Berry, is fed up slaving away under a glass ceiling for her bosses who won't make her a partner, and so is a ripe target for Davis as he continues to plan for his retirement. The question is, can he turn her allegiance to his own advantage and perhaps give her an opportunity to fleece her latest, and most odious, client Monroe, Tate Donovan? Lou, Mark Ruffalo, is the cop charged with trying to make headway investigating the robberies and it's him who concludes that Route 101 is crucial to the pattern and that his perpetrator is no ordinary thug. Scene set, what plays out now is a really quite disappointing drama that focuses too much on the characters and not enough on the mischievous intrigues and execution of the heists until the last ten minutes, when it finally comes alive a little. Hemsworth looks the part but doesn't really embrace it, Barry could have had more of the game but her part is left sadly undercooked. Keoghan just sticks to his tried and tested borderline maniacal role, only this time with dyed blonde hair. And finally there is Ruffalo who could have made for a more formidable foil for Hemsworth had their duel of wits been allowed more prominence. It does look good with Hemsworth looking every inch as if he'd stepped directly out from one of his many luxury goods adverts, but the remainder makes for a routinely charisma-free, car chase crime caper that I shall never remember. The aptly named Crime 101 looks a lot like any by the numbers entry-level script for an action crime drama slash thriller. There's exactly nothing new on offer here. Unless you are 100% new to the genre, this film will feel overly familiar, tired, predictable, and ultimately cliched. Dropping in a cast of well-known faces does nothing to fix the lack of originality on offer here. I managed a little over half of this flick before remembering I only had one life and didn't want to waste it watching the same thing over and over again, ad nauseum. It's been said that crime doesn't pay, but, as this notion is often portrayed in the movies, that's only true if one gets caught. Perpetrators skilled in covering their tracks frequently manage to find a way around the law, provided, of course, that they're truly adept at managing to stay ahead of authorities. That theory gets seriously put to the test in this third feature outing from writer-director Bart Leighton, the story of a slick, enigmatic, unassuming Los Angeles jewel thief, Chris Hemsworth, who's an expert at what he does, successfully pulling off his lucrative exploits without getting caught and without anyone getting hurt. But, in his latest job, wrinkles emerge that prompt him to reassess his circumstances, not to mention his future. These conditions uncharacteristically force him to improvise to stay ahead of those pursuing him, namely, an unconventional but insightful detective, Mark Ruffalo, an incisive insurance agent who specializes in managing the assets of wealthy clients, Halle Berry, and an undisciplined rival thief, Barry Kiyogan, tapped by his partner-in-cum, Nick Nolte, when the master criminal appears to be losing his nerve. Everyone here has a stake in how matters play out, both personally and professionally, but knowing how to proceed and who to trust become ever more complicated. In some respects, as this film's title implies, the narrative underlying this story could arguably be seen as somewhat generic as far as heist movies are concerned. However, there are elements in play here that help to elevate this release above many others in this genre. For instance, the degree of character development is greater than what one typically finds in pictures like this, as virtually all the players here are imbued with more depth and nuance than usual. Then there are the film's impressive production values, decidedly superior to many comparable offerings in such areas as cinematography, film editing, especially in the riveting car chases, and atmospheric background score. And, of course, the performances of the fine ensemble featured here do much to help set this release apart from its cinematic peers. Admittedly, several aspects of this production could use some shoring up, particularly in the areas of pacing, especially in the middle, and the development of a few of the picture's less important story threads. On balance, though, Crime 101 is a cut above what viewers might generally expect out of an offering like this, making for an enjoyable time at the movies, even if it's not overly original or particularly innovative. But this is one release that successfully finds ways to get away with it, and there's no crime in that.

Some movies seem destined for mixed reactions. That may be somewhat apparent before their release, but it invariably surfaces once in distribution. And it would seem to be very much the case with the latest and long-awaited release from writer-director Alejandro G. in Arie 2, a project that has been heavily promoted for some time. To complicate matters, Digger is a film that could easily fall prey to spoilers if too much is revealed in advance, a point decisively driven home and a caution posted on screen before the pictures start at press previews, so I apologize in advance if this analysis seems somewhat cryptic or evasive. The film primarily follows the wily exploits of Digger Rockwell, Tom Cruise in his first return to a character who essentially isn't an action-adventure hero since Magnolia, 1999, an aging, loud-mouthed good ol' boy oil tycoon who is one of the most powerful men in the world. He's good friends with the equally boisterous President Compson, John Goodman in what is arguably the best performance of his career, a bot and paid-for politician who conveys an impression of independence but is nevertheless quietly beholden to the protagonist and the commodity his corporation controls. But, for all the power these two colleagues wield, even their considerable resources and responsiveness are taxed when an explosion on a Greenland drilling tract leased to Digger's company triggers an environmental emergency. The detachment of an enormous ice shelf destined for collision with Northern Europe. And, since Digger is responsible for the disaster and whatever fallout stems from the actions of his American company, how are he and Compson supposed to respond? But that's only the half of what's transpiring here, and that's where those spoilers come into play. What's more, this is also where the mixed reactions to this offering are most likely to emerge. Indeed, to say more would reveal too much, but suffice it to say that the movie takes a radical turn at this juncture, one that some may find hard to follow initially, even though this shift is not entirely unexpected given that it recalls similar changes found in some of the filmmakers' previous pictures, like Birdman, 2014, and Bardo, 2022. While some of this could probably have been handled differently and better, the overall narrative nevertheless makes for an intriguing story filled with insightful, if familiar, messages about environmental decline, the unchecked power of big business, greedy CEOs and compromised politicians, and a public that often complains but takes few meaningful steps to counteract any of the foregoing. The picture could have also used a little less shouting, not only in the character's dialogue, but also in the conveyance of its sentiments. The writing has its strong points, especially in its piercing one-liners and pointed contentions, and the performances are generally solid, including those by the leads and supporting cast members Riz Ahmed, Sandra Holler, Michael Stulbar, and Jesse Plemons. But the biggest drawback in this satire is that there's really no one to pull for, and that keeps me at least from giving this release a stronger endorsement. Perhaps it would take another viewing to recommend it more enthusiastically. But that would undoubtedly take some digging.

A Disclosure Day is a fascinating, deeply hopeful return to sci-fi for Steven Spielberg, beautifully championing the concept of truth as a fundamental human right. Subverting the destructive tropes of typical alien invasion flicks, it favors radical empathy and genuine human connection over blockbuster chaos. Emily Blunt delivers a sensational, potentially career-best performance that anchors a truly incredible ensemble cast. Driven by exceptional camera work and a sweeping pace, it stands as one of my favorite films of the year so far. I cannot wait to see it again.

Director Steven Spielberg's filmography is legendary, to say the least. Movies like Jaws, 1975, Close Encounters of the Third Kind, 1977, Raiders of the Lost Ark, 1981, E.T., The Extraterrestrial, 1982, Schindler's List, 1993, and Jurassic Park, 1993, have gone down as classics in the annals of filmmaking. And, even though some of his works in more recent years haven't quite lived up to the quality of past efforts, it's comforting to know that he's still got what it takes when he gets behind the camera. This is where his latest release, Disclosure Day, comes into play, easily his best picture in years. This sci-fi-slash-conspiracy-theory-slash-personal-discovery thriller sports a multifaceted narrative that's probably too complex to detail here, but that's likely to be beneficial to viewers who walk into the theatre knowing little, if anything about it in advance. In fact, I'd actually recommend approaching this offering from that standpoint to allow it to wash over you organically, to experience and wrap yourself up in the sense of awe and wonder it evokes without the hindrance of too many preconceptions. The one thing I will say about it is that it's more than just another picture about UFOs and space aliens. While it's true that formal disclosure about the coverup of an extraterrestrial presence on earth over the past 80 years is at the core of the storyline, there's much more going on here, imbuing the title with multiple meanings involving other subjects, including those of a personal and spiritual nature, adding depth to what might have otherwise been merely a more conventional science fiction movie. This becomes apparent through the film's myriad story threads, which start out seeming disparate and unrelated, much like what happened at the beginning of Close Encounters. But, as this picture unfolds, connections develop showing how they all ultimately coalesce, just like in its predecessor. Some have called this kind of storytelling improbable and unrealistic, but many of us have undoubtedly seen this happen in our own lives, and, when that occurs, it doesn't seem nearly so far-fetched, so why should it be any different in a work of cinematic fiction? Of course, grasping the connections, nuances and meanings in this requires devoting sufficient attention when watching the movie, so, if you're unable or unwilling to do so for a film with a 2 hours and 25 minutes runtime, you might want to skip this one. That would be regrettable, though, given that Spielberg is back at the top of his game here, telling a story with the same skills he has brought to so many other releases over the years in terms of depicting a compelling plot, building suspense, executing gripping action sequences and providing appropriately timed comic relief. He also provides a comprehensive palette of ufology-related topics, some of which are well-known and others of which are more obscure, references that fans of Coast to Coast AM radio and the X-Files TV series will surely appreciate, but all of which are sufficiently explained without requiring ample viewer foreknowledge. And Spielberg has a lot of help bringing all this into being thanks to the insightful screenplay of David Kep, the original score of composer John Williams, arguably his most mature work ever, and the superb performances of an ensemble cast featuring Emily Blunt, Josh O'Connor, Colin Firth, Coleman Domingo, Eve Hewson, Wyatt Russell and Elizabeth Marvel. I'd heartily recommend watching this on as large a screen as possible, e.g., IMAX, and please pay no heed to the trolls voicing their uninformed opinions in trying to inexplicably tear this one down. Disclosure Day is about as nearly a perfect piece of filmmaking as one can envision. In fact, if I had to register a complaint of any kind here, it might be that the final act could be seen as being a little stretched out, but that's such a minor criticism that it's hardly worth mentioning. Savour all of the various forms of disclosure being served up in this. Release, as you may end up drawing upon them to discover aspects about yourself that you never knew before, and enabling you to walk out of the theatre at the end a different person than who you were when you went in and into a different world than what you knew before.

JJ Abrams-style lens flares all over the place that were nothing but distracting. The CG animals looked fake. The scenes that were supposed build tension were boring and predictable. Who could've guessed the aliens would look like that? Sarcasm. Since I worked at NBC's 30 Rock, I just had to laugh at how fake that was. Even John Williams' soundtrack had no oomph.

a movie made by dinosaurs, for the dinosaurs I wanted to like Disclosure Day. The premise, a government agent racing to expose classified alien contact, should be tense, urgent, relevant. Instead, what we get is a film so divorced from how the actual world works that it feels like it was written by people who've been in a bunker since 1987. The core problem, when your protagonist needs to leak classified information in 2026 or whenever this is supposed to happen, why in God's name are we watching them scheme about getting it done through a newsroom? The movie shows thumb drives, AI, all this modern tech, and then treats a television newsroom like it's the only lever that matters. It's nonsensical. If you want to burn a government secret to the world, you don't need Walter Cronkite anymore. There are better platforms on the internet. The infrastructure exists. The filmmakers simply have no clue how modern information systems work. And then there's the blandness. The villains have no depth, why do they actually care about keeping this secret? The heroes have no passion, what's driving them besides a vague sense of duty? There's no tension, no stakes that feel real, no reason to invest in anyone on screen. It's hollow. The whole thing is just hollow. Disclosure day isn't terrible. It's worse, it's boring. Please let it remain undisclosed.

Daniel, Josh O'Connor, has a narrow escape from the nasty Noah, Colin Firth, who wants to get back a mysterious glowing device that he has pinched. Meantime, television weather forecaster Margaret, Emily Blunt, takes a bit of a turn. Inexplicably, she can now speak fluent Korean and then passes out at the prospect of telling Kansans that Hale is looming. How could these two events possibly be connected? Well that's what we find out as the mother of all, very extended and somewhat repetitive. Car Chases gradually fills us in on a plan being coordinated by Hugo Colman Domingo, the only man so far who actually needed to speak with an American accent that isn't really understood by anyone, including himself. Is there something extraterrestrial afoot here? All the while the world is facing another existential crisis over some military antics on the Korean peninsula and so maybe mankind is doomed anyway and all this burning rubber is for naught? This film is a wet dream for conspiracy theorists the world over, but with little by way of characterization it's lacking in depth, detail, humor, or soul. It's overly trading on the name of its director slash writer and relying on some visual and occasional animatronic effects that we've been getting more and more used to ever since ET 40 odd years ago. This isn't a bad film, it just isn't a very good one and I reckon nobody will remember it for long. It is a cinema must, though, if you do want to see it. Perhaps Jane, Eve Hewson, is the character with the biggest arch but we don't get a lot of time with her. It makes the whole thing run like molasses at times in the middle as they just seem to be checking off the boxes of plot exposition. I also didn't like the cat and mouse play between Noah, Colin Firth, and our two main characters Margaret, Emily Blunt, and Daniel, Josh O'Connor. It's confusing at first, then it makes sense, and then they use it too much to the point it just drags. The film somehow manages to come together for a roller coaster finale. The sloppy and seemingly rushed threads come together for something that definitely hits hard and is more concentrated and developed than the early parts of the film. I found myself at full attention as the film began firing on all cinematic cylinders for its conclusion. Overall I'm happy I saw it but it's probably gonna be my only watch for disclosure. This probably would have worked better as a series so the characters and ideas could be developed a bit more. We do get what could be John Williams' last score. I made sure I stayed for the whole credits roll.

Score, 3 out of 10, a fictional misstep in a moment demanding truth for the average moviegoer, this film would probably gain a higher score. It has the Spielberg pedigree, a solid cast led by the fantastic Emily Blunt, and a chase-thriller structure that delivers some entertainment. But for those of us who sit where we do on the precipice of actual disclosure, deeply invested in the reality of UAPs and non-human intelligence, NHI, this film is an extremely flawed and very disappointing experience. The most frustrating part is its premise. The film explores a what-if scenario of a public unveiling of alien secrets, but given where we are in the world today, this is not the right time for a fictitious movie on this topic to be released. Half the population of the planet believes that we are not alone and are looking for answers, the real-world conversation is finally shifting, driven by congressional hearings, whistleblower testimonies, and a slow trickle of government acknowledgement. Releasing a heavily fictionalized, melodramatic thriller during this fragile moment feels not just unhelpful, but almost exploitative. I can watch a movie like E.T., the extraterrestrial and be thoroughly entertained because it is very clearly a film made for entertainment, with an entertaining plot. Disclosure Day, on the other hand, is not just entertainment for many people. It draws directly on real-world themes, the tic-tac sightings, the Roswell narrative, the 2023 congressional hearings using them as a launchpad for a film that one critic called flimsy and outdated. The result is a film that feels caught between wanting to be a serious meditation on the topic and delivering a generic chase movie that has no ideas about aliens that we haven't heard before. The plot is a mess. A whistleblower's plan to leak evidence depends on a local TV news broadcast, which feels like a plot device from the 1980s. There are seemingly pointless supernatural elements, such as a crop circle magically forms around Daniel with no explanation. The film's focus on the chase means the thought-provoking elements are sacrificed for action that one review called a drabex files episode. The ending, in which Margaret delivers the one-word message listen to the world, feels more like a pretentious cliffhanger than a profound statement. The hope is that we can separate the real, unfolding history from this reductive, fictional placeholder. The Verdict Disclosure Day is a film that misunderstands its moment. For those of us deep in the rabbit hole of UFOs and NHI, you're better off not watching this movie. The real story is far more fascinating and unfolding in real time. This film is a hollow echo of a conversation that has finally started to get serious. Watch if asterisk you are an average moviegoer looking for an undemanding Spielberg thriller and can ignore the real-world context. Skip if asterisk you follow the UAP topic closely. The subplots and storylines are extremely flawed and very disappointing. The search for truth is better served by documentaries and congressional hearings than this reductive movie.

Spielberg's fade to black Daniel, Josh O'Connor, is a cybersecurity analyst who stumbles upon classified video files proving the government has been capturing and torturing non-human beings ever since the Roswell incident. After becoming a digital fugitive, he joins forces with Margaret Fairchild, Emily Blunt, a TV meteorologist experiencing strange perceptual phenomena. Together, they launch a race against time to expose the existence of alien life to the world, all while escaping the clutches of an implacable government contractor played by Colin Firth, who is hell-bent on stopping the uncontrolled leak of these files. Disclosure Day marks Steven Spielberg's long-awaited return to alien contact sci-fi, a genre where he previously gifted us absolute masterpieces like Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Unfortunately, this piece of work feels way more like an exercise in self-indulgence than a fresh, modern take. The first hour of the feature film works quite well as a corporate conspiracy thriller. The protagonist's pursuit maintains a tense pace, and the cinematography is, predictably, top-tier, complete with its fair share of absurd details and inexplicable plot holes, of course. However, as the plot drags on, David Kep's script gets tangled up in pseudoscientific nonsense about childhood trauma and the main character's psychic abilities, completely draining the urgency from their very escape. The film's fatal flaw lies in its high and mighty moral and philosophical pretensions. Spielberg gets so incredibly bogged down in emphasizing the importance of faith, communication, and humanity's place in the universe that he forgets to give the audience any sort of satisfying resolution. Deliberately cutting the climax short just to fade to black after the word listen is nowhere near a poetic, cinematic stroke of freaking genius. It's just a cheap trick to avoid answering the questions we spent over two hours setting up.

Watching Evil Dead Burn becomes an ordeal that tests how close the line between the MPAA's R and NC-17 ratings can be pushed like no other horror film seen this year and maybe several years before. Assaulting audiences with tongue-in-cheek, stomach-churning horror has long been the hallmark of Sam Raimi's Evil Dead franchise since Bruce Campbell first fired up his chainsaw and declared it groovy nearly 40 years ago. In director Sebastian Vanechek's hands, after Raimi hand-picked him for this latest outing following his skin-crawling French-language debut Infested, 2023, there is more humor but also far more cruelty than any prior film in the franchise. As with Evil Dead Rise, there is a somewhat disconnected intro equally horrific before the main story settles in, where the central cast, Suhaila Youkube, Hunter Dewan, Lucien Buchanan, experience graphic and disturbing violence that may make some audiences sick to their stomachs. As the Deadites descend upon a dilapidated, rural family home and a grieving family led by a young widow, the sheer amount of cruelty each of the characters endures is at times overwhelming. In one particular moment, a dinner scene around the family dining table is especially cruel and wince-inducing. But for the use of some well-timed gallows humor, the whole affair might have otherwise seemed like something out of the blood-soaked dreams of St. Thomas Aquinas. With a threadbare plot, gnarly vignettes of escalating brutality, fans of the practical effects Raimi first introduced to audiences in 1981 will surely embrace this latest offering for all its coagulated gore. But underneath the pools of blood and viscera is Youkube's earnest portrayal of Alice, whose ordeal throughout the movie is an empowering example of triumphing over spousal abuse and generational trauma. When the end inevitably comes asterisk but wait. There's more. A mid-credits scene and a substantial post-credits scene that's worth the wait if you still have the stomach for it, asterisk you may leave the cinema drained from the graphic catharsis of enduringness. If Evil Dead films have always been about pushing the envelope Evil Dead Burn may get the distinction of pushing it further than any of its predecessors. Errol Shand, Greta Van Den Brink, Tandy Wright and Ma David co-star.

This is a worthy successor to the franchise, and it does a lot of fun with the source material. The characters are fun, which means that you get to engage with them and feel something when they meet their gruesome demise, which is way better than having interchangeable teens just being lost instantly when in some cabin somewhere. The movie has plenty of fun gore and intricate kills and does not lose sight of its core narrative. It's claustrophobic and very tightly shot, and the post-credit murder is fantastic, calling back to Evil Dead Rise.

The film strikes a great balance, delivering clever narrative tiebacks to Evil Dead Rise alongside a subtle, underlying connection to the lore of the original films. Rather than resting on nostalgia, it uses those classic elements to build a story that feels fresh while remaining distinctly true to the franchise's roots. The shift in setting works brilliantly here. Moving the terror out of Rise's cramped city apartment block and into a sprawling, secluded farmhouse gives the film a completely different kind of claustrophobia. The rural atmosphere and isolated location gave off massive Resident Evil 7, biohazard Baker family vibes. That uncomfortable sense of being trapped with a deeply unhinged, hostile family dynamic long before the supernatural madness even takes over. When the deadites do unleash, the film delivers in spades. Modern Evil Dead entries have really amped up the brutal, relentless nature of the gore, and burn is no exception. What makes it work so well is the sheer tactile impact of the set pieces. Between the aggressive sound design and a reliance on heavy practical effects over cheap digital tricks, every injury, splash of blood, and horrific transformation feels uncomfortably real and punishing. It's really encouraging to see movies like this succeeding, especially since horror felt like it was going through a bit of a dry spell recently. We're finally getting a steady stream of inventive, high-quality genre films that actually respect the audience and make the trip to the cinema worthwhile. I'd highly recommend Evil Dead Burn to any horror fan. The best way to experience these modern entries is to disconnect them from Raimi's 80s originals. Those were iconic products of their time, whereas this current era is leaning into dark, visceral, unfiltered horror. Both eras are brilliant in their own right, and Burn proves this franchise still has plenty of gas in the tank.

One such trip involves the pair travelling to Thailand and walking a precarious route four thousand feet above sea level to visit a sacred dragon that will eat all of their fears. Turning up, they discover that this route has been deemed unsafe by the authorities and that it's a no-go area. Foiled? Well, no, they meet John, Tom Brittany, who offers to guide them for five thousand dollars. A bit steep? Yes, but not as steep as the ladder up the cliffs to a rotting wooden path supported by scaffolding poles, allegedly built by monks decades ago. This area is prone to earthquakes, so guess what happens as they meander along towards the devil's elbow? Actually, to be fair to this it's not its predictability that lets it down. That has to be the responsibility of a writer who has produced some of the most banal dialogue ever to hit the silver screen and to some acting that, even when precariously perched on a plank of wood, doesn't convey any sense of fear or peril whatsoever. The last twenty minutes would actually be comical if they weren't so risible, and that That sense of acrophobic menace that existed in the first film, 2022, is distinctly lacking as the twists in this story fail to resonate plausibly. Even the photography looks as if the camera had been turned on its side, and at no point did I actually believe that anyone had ever left the ground for this, even the drone pilot. This will look fine on the television on a winter's Friday night after some vino, but you'll never need to watch it twice.

Forgotten_Island.transcribe: Wapush! DreamWorks' Forgotten Island delivers everything I expected, glorious animation with some really cool anime references, hilarious jokes and physical comedy, strong character bonds and interactions, powerful, tear-jerking emotional scenes, immersive world-building, and an upbeat soundtrack that rivals even the likes of K-pop demon hunters. This movie's story which is all about the fear of separation between best friends Joe and Vrisa reminds me of my own friendship with my best friend Christopher Capone and how he moved away but we stayed together as besties even after that moment happened. The Nikali Island characters are also really fun and full of personality, although Man in Angle and Ra are my favorites. I honestly almost wanted to hate Dave Franco after Hoppers but Ra got me reinvested. And having the movie end with both Man in Angle and Badaba redeem themselves by giving back people's items to ensure their memories remain intact really shows that DreamWorks has the guts to pull off the same levels of emotional storytelling Pixar gives us while at the same time providing a great parallel to Joe's decision to let Raissa attend college in America. Speaking of that ending, it made me cry really hard. Please do not sleep on this movie. It is a true gem to behold.

GOAT.transcribe: The Thorns aren't doing so well in the Roarball League despite the presence of the legendary Leopard Jet, so when owner Flo sees a video of the feisty young goat will giving one of the sport's other celebrities mayn a run for his money, she decides to sign him up. It's a combination of American football and basketball, it's quickly paced and occasionally violent so needless to say Captain Jet isn't impressed with their diminutive and attitudinal young signing. Initially, the whole team are fairly disdainful of their new buddy and she leaves him on the bench, but with the team still struggling maybe it's time to let him try to prove his worth? This is all fairly procedural stuff and I didn't love the style of animation, it seemed a little jittery to me and the perspective looked a bit all over the place at times as the story touches predictably on elements of adulation, aspiration, team playing, trust and even some good old greed as it marches along for I felt was quite a long hundred minutes. Aside from the goat and the leopard, there isn't really much effort put into characterizing the other teammates and it could have had more fun with aspects of just how ruthless and venal the business of global sport can be, win or lose, which could have added a bit of depth to it. It's watchable enough and the plucky will is quite engaging, but it's nothing special.

I am very split on this movie. It's not bad, but also nothing special. First off, the visuals and character designs are lovely. Like several recent Sony animations movies, this one was visually really nice and the animations were nice once you get used to the stuttering animation style. Similar to Super Team 4 or the combat scenes from Puss in Boots, The Last Wish. The general story is the really basic underdog or undergoat story including all of its tropes and stereotypes. Person with the wrong size slash race slash species slash upbringing wants to do skill x, everyone laughs about them. Until they show them they're awesome at it. Done for every sport, every craft, etc. That's not bad, per se. The problem for me is mainly the movie's first half. You know how these movies always have that one angry, asshole person that tells the protagonist they're never gonna make it, that never takes them for serious? Like Tigress in Kung Fu Panda and every rival in underdog movies? Officially that's Jet in this movie. But factually it's everyone in the first half, except the main character's best friends. And while having one doubting ass can be a cool thing to overcome, having basically a whole team's personalities reduced to you don't care about this guy made me really wonder if the movie will feature any non-assholes at all. As soon as the second half starts, the moment where the protagonist finally shows off his skills and the characters suddenly get actual personality, the whole movie becomes much better. Sadly this happens far too late, and instead of showing so long-winded how nobody thinks he can do it, they should have cut that short and instead used the free time to draw out the actual emotional scenes longer. Because those have potential and show much more personality, but one very important emotional part is even cut short into a montage, and that's just really a pity. In addition, based on the German dub, the movie heavily relies on modern youth slang. To me this felt very, well, cringe. But I accept that I'm most likely not the target audience and I'm willing to take a seat and accept that it's a thing of the current time which I'm not a part of anymore, so I won't judge that harshly. Grinning face with sweat oh, also, gods, so many product placements. I'm used to Xperia phones in Sony movies, but damn, phones, these cars, clothes, I hate product placement in movies, and here several camera shots were very obviously done just to show off brand logos. So, yeah. The movie is fine. It gets much better once the characters finally show personality and get emotional. This should happen much earlier and deeper because it was when the movie was its strongest. The story combines every single underdog movie trope and features every underdog character stereotype. If you're fine with that, I'd say watch the movie for its cool visuals. Not necessarily in an expensive cinema, though. All that said, the diner sheep is a lovely motherly figure, I like her. Modo is fucked up in all the best ways possible. And the Aardwolf girl Hannah is the cutest, coolest, most awesome character, and I want more of her. Red heart.

Sony Pictures' animation is still the GOAT of making stylized animated movies, because this one was extremely entertaining. On the surface, it feels like a typical underdog movie small protagonist tries to prove himself, a major team gives him a position, they all win it's pretty much laid out there from the start. But that's where things change. You see, once the main character of GOAT, Will Harris, joins the Thorns, his favorite roarball team, yes, that's what they call basketball in this movie, it stops being about Will trying to prove to his team he is a great addition and starts being more about teamwork. That is what separates GOAT from other underdog sports movies, and what makes it so entertaining from start to finish. The animation, of course, is really awesome, it's very funny, has lots of emotion, and a stellar voice cast. Oh, and the soundtrack is lit. GOAT is definitely gonna be one of my favorite movies of this year, and maybe in general. Who knows.

Anyone remember one man and his dog on the telly? Well instead of a sheepdog, this introduces us to Odin, an highly trained military canine that's clearly had a fairly torrid time and is now in the care of his Earthswile Sergeant James, Brad Pitt. James has his own little Cessna and loves nothing more than to set off into the Alaskan wilderness to get back to nature. He, too, is not without his wartime injuries and it's while he is trying to outfly a storm that his plane ends up in a lake. Now the pair have to make it across 60 miles of inhospitable terrain and avoid some wolves and bears if they are to make it to the nearest road. What ensues illustrates the affection and interdependence of both of these characters as they struggle against adversity and injury but I think my problem here was that word character. We don't really get to know much about James at all and so are largely left with an updated version of Incredible Journey, 1963, only with far improved photography of their pristine and unforgiving environment. Oddly enough for a film that can't have had many budget issues, the CGI effects aren't the best and the whole thing just came across as a little too earnest a project for me. Pitt and director David Ayer clearly have points to make in the ethics of using animals as weapons of war, as well as the provision of aftercare for all who fought and returned traumatized to varying degrees and who were left to reintegrate into a society for which they are now ill-equipped are a couple that are raised quite poignantly at times but again we are given too little context beyond a few violent flashbacks to put some roots onto their obvious bond. Their constant frying pan to fire scenarios also begin to stretch the bounds of plausibility and some of the continuity simply doesn't add up either. In some ways I almost wished this were just a documentary of a survival story that we could observe without feeling any need to invest in James but instead I found this just a little too short on depth and maybe just a little too sentimental. It does remind us of just how puny mankind is when we are exposed, largely unarmed and unpampered, to nature on its terms and Pitt certainly convinces on the strenuous effort front but I just wanted a little more story. Hope.transcribe: An old saying maintains never put the cart before the horse, an observation whose implications should be obvious. That applies in filmmaking, too, when a standalone production is thought to be the inspiration for a new franchise, the creators need to be careful not to get ahead of themselves. That's to say that the first film in the proposed series absolutely must be a knockout to earn the right to a sequel, or sequels, Star Trek notwithstanding. But, if those behind the initial effort are so focused on what lies down the road in a potential franchise that they don't get the first release right, it's the equivalent of shooting themselves in the foot. And that is precisely what undermines this latest release from writer-director Na Hing-jin. In essence, this sci-fi action adventure follows the improbable, occasionally strangely madcap attempts by a small-town South Korean police force and others to hunt down a mysterious monster that's wreaking all manner of havoc in their community and the surrounding environment. The problem, though, is that little is explained as the story unfolds, with an array of tropes that seem unconscionably thrown together, virtually no backstory, a disjointed, poorly constructed narrative, woefully cheap CGI, a plot based almost entirely on clichés, frenetic action sequences, and absurd, sometimes patently inappropriate comic relief, and more overused expletives than seen in The Wolf of Wall Street, 2013. While the film admittedly gets off to a reasonably well-managed start, coming across as a fusion between the Godzilla movies and the folksy, homespun nature of Fargo, 1996, it's an opening act that's ultimately unforgivably drawn out. Building suspense is one thing, but knowing that a big reveal is coming and taking 45 minutes to get there is a bit much. And, sadly, things go downhill from there, with a story that makes little sense stretched out to a stunning 2 hours and 39 minutes runtime, overstaying its welcome by nearly an hour. My only hope for the picture at that point was that it was mercifully heading to wrap things up with some kind of coherent explanation that, unfortunately, never comes. And that's where the focus of what's to be included in future franchise installments intrudes upon the credibility and integrity of this release. What's even more mystifying here is the high praise that this overlong saga has received both in critics' circles and at the prestigious Cannes Film Festival, where hope was inexplicably awarded a Palme d'Or nomination, the event's highest honour. Moviegoers looking for entertaining scary fare along these lines have so many other, better choices to draw from, such as Jaws, 1975, Jurassic Park, 1993, and the recently released The End of Oak Street, 2026. Please, watch one of those titles instead.

The discovery of a badly mauled cow is quite perplexing for the local police chief, Huang Yongmin, especially when a few of his wisecracking citizens suggest it might have been caused by a marauding tiger. It doesn't take him long to realize that whatever it is, it's a great deal bigger and more menacing than a cat as he returns to town and finds scenes of death and destruction with gunfire sounding regularly. What are they shooting at? Meantime, out in the woods his group of mischievous tiger hunters are finding themselves embroiled in something altogether more mysterious, extraterrestrial and perilous too. Okay, so it is far too long and for much of the later stages it reminded me of an hybrid of that lackluster 65, 2023 and Predator, 1987, only with some added semi-slapstick comedy, but the first hour is quickly paced and entertaining end-to-end stuff. There's a bit of comedy horror, some welcome sarcasm delivered front and center of the pithy and earthy script and the fact that we don't encounter their powerful new foe for almost all of that phase of the film manages to build an enjoyable sense of anticipation. Just what could be tossing people and cars so effortlessly? Once we meet their new nemesis, however, this plot quickly starts to lose its sharpness and actually, despite a lively effort from the feisty Sung-A-E, Hoi-Yon, becomes just a little too repetitious. Seemingly endless supplies of ammunition and never-ending empty roads start to give the film a distinctly video game feel supported by some CGI that can be a little ropey at times. The really quite disappointing conclusion left me wondering whether they just ran out of filming days or whether there might be plans for a sequel if this does well enough at the box office, but in any event it doesn't really satisfy and the few clues we are given about their visitors and their motivation are oblique at best. There's no denying that it's good fun to watch, though, with plenty of action, explosives and even a few horses, but it could have lost 45 minutes and been none the worse for it.
