Hoppers.transcribe: I really liked this movie, the best Pixar movie in years for me. To be fair, maybe that's just because of me being an environmentalist myself, but hey, in the end, reviews here are supposed to be subjective, I guess. Mabel, the main character, is a lovely main character. An environmentalist since childhood, depicted by her actions of demonstrating, collecting signatures, blocking building sites and even being carried away by police. And while all of this is depicted in a funny, child-friendly way, it does actually do a nice job of displaying her doing all the things an environmentalist encounters. She's friendly, dedicated and, oh no, that one in a bit. First, visually, the movie is, as one is used from Pixar, beautiful. Lovely hairs and fur, beautiful water and dam, clothes, single strands of fabric, it's so beautiful and detailed. Everything that is not a character is so detailed and visually impressive. Not to say the characters don't look nice, though. The humans are fine, the animals are lovely and cuddly, and, in case that's a thing that matters for you, it's not a movie to use the infamous bean-mouth design. I think, many jokes are quick and funny, the trailers showed the humor quite well as a reference to what to expect. The messages are what you'd expect, humans destroying animals' home in their greed and ignorance, how nature as a whole is one big thing, including humans, and that everyone should do their part. And here are the two things that make the movie really important and lovely for me personally. The thing that we're all part of something bigger, something we're in together, all creatures, is an important part of my life. It's why I love the message of Cici and Isawa, we are the same, in Lion Guard so much. To see humans not as a single thing, but as the part we are with all other creatures. And in addition, and that's the other part of Mabel that is depicted nicely, but I still wish had gotten more time, the constant feeling of sadness and anger that you get thinking that you are the only one that cares about something that is so important to you. And that's really why I love her, because she's so relatable to me as environmentalist and vegan. The music in the movie is also really nice, and really the only downside I can see is, I wish it was half an hour or so longer. More time to depict Mabel's feeling of being alone and misunderstood, more time to show how humans forcefully change nature and of course a bit more time for the hilarious chase scene. So, yeah. I wish the movie did more of what it does, because it does it so well. I really enjoyed the movie and I wish its message, as peaceful as it was, sadly, transported, would stick with anyone longer than the cinema visit. I recommend this. And greetings to my fellow environmentalists. You're not alone, just like Mabel isn't. Red heart.

The town's mayor wants to build a beltway around his city, and it's almost complete. The only missing segment is over a lake that has been dammed by some now absent beavers. Mabel is determined to thwart the constructors, but with all the animal life having seemingly relocated to pastures slash ponds new there seems little she can do to stop their dynamiting. Then she learns that if she can reintroduce some wild critters to the waters, then it will be saved. How, though? Well one evening she espies one, but it doesn't like the look of the new surroundings and moves on. She follows it and after a bit of subterfuge, finds herself in a secret laboratory where her college teacher has perfected a scientific technique to link human brains to robotic bodies and so recreate animal. Mabel is not to be stopped on her quest, and so promptly finds herself with a new fur coat and introduced to the mammal king George who now hosts all the displaced from the motorway. She knows that she must get him and his fellow monarchs from above and below the water to ally if she is to have any chance of restoring the equilibrium of nature. What chance she can rally them all to defeat the bulldozers, though? The environmental message is all pretty blunt, but it is delivered in an amiable fashion with some fun and puns from the writing, a lovely scene depicting regal succession in the insect world and even a flying shark as we are gently reminded that humanity is but one of the creatures that lives on our earth. This also manages to stay clear of sentimentality, not always so easy when the plot is all about all things furry, feathery or fishy, and it's also refreshing in its targeting of the civic administration as the baddie here, rather than just opting for those pesky and evil corporate types. Ice_Cream_Man.transcribe: There are films that are so bad they're good. Then there are films that are simply bad. And then, right at the bottom of the barrel, there are films that aren't merely bad but deeply offensive. Ice Cream Man is what Eli Roth has scraped from beneath that barrel. Remember Hostel? One of Roth's earliest films, it caused such a furor that it helped popularize an entire subgenre, torture porn. Yet, for all its reputation, Roth actually demonstrated considerable restraint. Some of its most frightening moments occur precisely when the camera turns away from the violence. His subsequent films, including Hostel, Part 2, The Green Inferno and Knock Knock, suggested a steady erosion of that restraint and a descent into gleeful gore, obnoxious provocation and increasingly cringe-worthy camp. There is plenty of all three in Ice Cream Man, and that is not necessarily a problem. Gore and Camp can be enormously entertaining when handled with wit, imagination or technical skill. Here, however, everything is executed so artlessly that the film quickly becomes numbing. The effects look fake, the dialogue is juvenile, and the characters are little more than bodies waiting to be dissected. The performances are uniformly amateurish, from adults and children alike. Even allowing for the leeway usually afforded to young actors, it is painfully apparent that Roth has no idea how to direct them. Nothing is shocking because nothing feels consequential. It is simply boring. The film never finds a workable pace or tone. It lurches constantly between idiotic adults walking willingly towards their deaths, extreme close-ups of mutilation and tedious scenes in which the child protagonists recite dialogue so insipid that it sounds as though they wrote it themselves, although that is probably an insult to child writers. One character, temporarily paralyzed, spends what feels like two solid minutes flopping from room to room like a landed fish. Whatever comic potential the sequence initially possesses is exhausted long before the scene ends. All of that would be disappointing enough. What makes Ice Cream Man genuinely enraging, however, is its relentless parade of offensive ideas masquerading as transgressive humor. A young woman is forced to promise that she will reconcile with her ex-boyfriend before he agrees to rescue her, and then she actually does. Pedophilia becomes the premise for a ludicrous comedy horror that never comes close to establishing a coherent tone. A protagonist casually uses the ableist arse-lure before another character turns autism into the punchline of the very next joke. In one grotesquely misjudged sequence, a black person is chained to the back of a truck and dragged along the ground, invoking the imagery of racist violence and lynching, seemingly in pursuit of one more cheap shock. But the piece to resistance, the final insult, the cherry on top, if you'll pardon the pun, is the moment when a child actor, in a film released in 2026, is made to utter the following appalling line, I'm a 12-year-old girl. Of course I know how to throw up. At that moment, it took everything I had not to get up and walk straight out of the cinema. Even by the low standards Roth has increasingly set for himself, Ice Cream Man is a disgrace. It is a film that mistakes misogyny for edginess, ableism for humor, and racist imagery for entertainment. Beneath all the gore and desperate provocation, there is no intelligence, no daring and no discernible humanity, just an ugly, witless film congratulating itself for having the nerve to be offensive.

Eli Roth's mean-spirited nature was present in the film, and it felt uncomfortable watching very young children commit violent acts, and a joke involving a 12-year-old girl's eating disorder. Oh, now come on, who hasn't enjoyed delicious mint Romney ice cream? Unfortunately, there is a side effect if you feed it to our children, it turns them into marauding murderers intent on killing every adult they see whether they be parent, guardian, granny, or teacher. Luckily, though, Jared, Charlie's elster, is lactose intolerant and his sister Lizzie, Sarah Abbott, won't let him have any. Phew! That leaves him, Mia, Kiori Mirza-Waldman, and Tommy, Shiloh O'Reilly, as the only kids in the town not determined on a rampage of gory slaughter. What's causing all of this? Well they, and we, quickly deduce that it must have something to do with the creepy ice cream man, Ari Millen, whose van appears at all hours of the day and night to top up their dose of cone delights and so fuel their antics even the hunky fireman isn't safe. After about 10 minutes, this descended into a most puerile and unsophisticated dose of CGI-driven nonsense that did, at least, invoke a degree of unanimity from the dozen or so of us in the cinema who were all looking at each other wondering how this ever got off the drawing board. It's repetitious, there's no jeopardy nor is there even the vaguest attempt to craft any characters that we might care less about as their killing spree finds as many ways of carving someone up and then sets it all to music. It's as if Messers Belson and Roth just typed the word kill into a digital thesaurus and then let their computers run riot with the results. To be fair to Zeltzer, he tries to inject a little stoic humanity into the proceedings even if his some of his riper dialogue uses language that people his own age wouldn't be able to sit on the other side of the screen and actually watch, but the remainder of the cast just look like they've been just been told to go make some mess for the cameras. Even Hammer or John Carpenter at their abject worst managed to keep us interested in what was happening to some extent, but this really hasn't anything to redeem it at all except perhaps the end credits. It smacks of something that someone might think has legs for another scoop, but I really hope those with the cash take a stance against such autotrash and invest in cinema that actually requires people to screw up rather than just our machines.

Insidious_Out_of_the_Further.transcribe: We discover from fairly early on that the young Gemma, Charlie Penton, is usually left to her own devices by her clearly distracted mother, so it's no surprise when we spin forward a generation and discover that she, now Amelie Eve, has had to deal with a fairly traumatic experience before going on to becoming a dentist and raising her own daughter Maya, Island Austin, in the very same house. She's been dating, on the quiet, the hunky cop Nick, Brandon Perez, and all in her life seemed stable until a visit to the basement with her child unearths some old family memorabilia and then things start going bump in her dreams. A terrifying experience in a pillow fort and an even more gruesome one in her own dental practice encourages her to seek advice from Claire, Maisie Richardson Sellers, who acts as a conduit to the world of the benign Elise, Lynn Shea, who explains something of the evil that is trying to escape from the further realm and invade the world of the living with a population of zombified and hungry corpses. It seems that Gemma has a special gift that has attracted this menace and that it won't stop until she stops it. How? Well that's going to involve convincing Maya and her boyfriend that she's not lost the plot and that the dangers are real. There are a few genuinely affecting scenes here, especially amidst the ostensible safety of cushions and sheets, but the rest of this lacks much by way of jeopardy. Regular watchers of these films will probably agree that the supposedly insurmountable barriers between the malignant, the nefarious, the past and the present all appear to be wafer thin with an all too familiar surfeit of connecting two-way red doors. The acting is all fine and some of the photography does help to craft a certain sense of peril, but this isn't so much insidious as straightforward and though it does have its moments, it's a franchise that has had its day and ought now to be put in a box of its own in the cellar with a label saying open in 50 years.

Insidious, Out of the Further isn't reinventing the wheel on its sixth go-around, but it delivers enough legitimate chills to earn its keep. Directed by Jacob Chase, the film shines brightest when it leans into surreal visual set pieces, including a nauseatingly tense dental chair sequence and a claustrophobic, spatial warping couch fort. Amelia Eve gives a strong, grounded lead performance, and Lynn Shea's return as Elise Renier provides the usual warm, ghostly nostalgia that ties the franchise together. Movie relies a bit too heavily on loud, predictable jump scares though. It doesn't reach the heights of James Wan's original films, but with solid lead performances and a few standout sequences, it's a fun, spooky ride that lands at a comfortable 7 out of 10.

It_Ends.transcribe: Open wide and still claustrophobic, it is a bit strange how an open road can feel claustrophobic, but it does. It is a well-acted movie, and while the plot is only there to allow for character exploration, and you never truly get to learn a whole lot about the actual setting, that's part of the idea. Resolutions are optional in such stories. The movie is by no means bad, but it is not one I will revisit and re-watch.

In the interest of full disclosure up front, I'll do my best to assess this release without being overly unkind. To be honest, this debut feature from writer-director Alexander Ullam has almost assuredly earned itself a spot on my worst of 2026 list. Loosely based on the 1944 existentialist stage play No Exit by Jean-Paul Sartre, it ends tells the story of four 20-something friends, a term I use loosely, Fina Hazioun, Mitchell Cole, Akira Jackson, Noah Toth, who embark on a late-night drive but soon find themselves lost on a never-ending highway through a thickly forested woodland from which there's no apparent escape, asterisk i.e. asterisk, no exit. In an effort to spice up the plot, the narrative subsequently attempts to infuse a few horror tropes, but, sadly, these poorly handled elements aren't particularly scary or the least bit enlightening in defining the essence of the plot. At one point, for instance, the puzzled quartet is attacked by a band of fleet-footed zombies, forcing the fearful foursome to flee for their lives. It's an element that's reincorporated or inferred throughout the film but that, frankly, has little ultimate bearing on the story. What's more, the sequence is so ineptly executed that it's ultimately more confusing than frightening. Not long thereafter, when matters settle down and these lost souls begin discussing the nature of their bewildering circumstances, they're forced to begin considering that they might be trapped in some kind of alternate existence, even a hellish version of the afterlife. That possibility, in turn, prompts yet another round of long-winded, uninteresting existential discussions that are part metaphysics, part petty bickering and part overwrought Generation Z angst, all set against the backdrop of an incessant road trip for which practical concerns like having enough fuel for the journey, wherever it may be headed, are apparently irrelevant. And that, in a nutshell, fittingly characterises the dynamics of this wholly pretentious offering, despite what may have started out with a worthwhile premise and good intentions. The blame here lies largely with the woefully undercooked, meandering screenplay. For example, most of the excessive group discussions are lame and unfocused and lack engaging substance, light years removed from the eloquence and insight of the source material that inspired this production. Then there's the seriously underused horror aspect, which might have added more interest if more skilfully and integrally employed. The filming techniques are also stunningly puzzling, with much of the action shot too dimly and or too up close, so much so that, in sequences like the zombie attack, it's difficult to tell what's happening. And, of course, there are plot holes aplenty, which are genuinely inexcusable, even for a first-time filmmaker. To its credit, though, the picture gets one thing right, it's a testament to Sartre's renowned contention that hell is other people, as these characters come to find out for themselves, bringing fresh meaning to that statement and to the audience, indeed, I can't imagine being stuck with individuals like these for eternity, 89 minutes was more than enough for me. But that spot on irony is not nearly enough to save this effort, especially since it even more ironically gives viewers reason to skip this release. Perhaps, as a senior, the generational nuances at work here were lost on me, but, that aside, while screening this offering, I also couldn't help but keep asking myself, are we there yet?

Sex is one of those subjects that can be difficult to address on film. It can easily come across as shallow, silly titillation, as body, shameless voyeurism, or as a veiled form of porn euphemistically garbed as a work of erotic art. What's more, viewers going into theaters to watch offerings about this subject may have expectations that don't reflect any of the foregoing examples or that don't live up to what they anticipate, leaving many audience members frustrated and disappointed. But, every so often, a movie comes along that gets things right, as is very much the case with the new comedy from writer-director Greg Araki. As the film's title unabashedly proclaims, this release is unapologetically about what it says it is, at least superficially. In actuality, however, there's much more to this offering than what it suggests, and that's what helps to make this an insightfully worthwhile watch, sexual considerations notwithstanding. In essence, the film follows the outrageous exploits of an outspoken, freewheeling, perpetually thirsty erotic artist, Erika Tracy, Olivia Wilde, and one of her naive, sheepish gallery assistants, Elliot Cooper-Hoffman, who engage in a wildly uninhibited relationship ostensibly built just on sex. In many ways, it's a scenario in which submissive, clueless Elliot finds himself in way over his head. However, as a recent college graduate in need of work, he takes the job, which, despite the considerable demands of his indisputably dominant boss, ironically ends up being quite liberating and erotically fulfilling, especially since his cold, perpetually indifferent girlfriend, Minerva, Charlie XCX, frequently leaves him and his needs unattended, prompting Elliot to engage in frequent acts of self-satisfaction. As time passes, though, relations between Erika and Elliot start to sour as he begins to take the nature of their relationship seriously, some might even say obsessively, something that she views as completely casual, easily dismissive and lacking in the same emotional intensity as her ever hopeful would-be suitor. And this, in turn, causes Elliot's life to fall apart on multiple fronts, even leading to specious suspicions involving murder raised by two perplexed, stone-faced detectives, Johnny Knoxville, Margaret Cho. What's perhaps most fascinating about this film, though, is the many issues it examines through the lens of sex. The relationship between Erika and Elliot may begin with and be rooted in sex, but it raises questions about such matters as honesty, trust, control and obsession, as well as the relationship dynamics of dom-subsexuality. The narrative also introduces passing but relevant observations about generational social attributes and how they're reflected through sexuality, just like virtually all other aspects of life. This makes for an incisive, smartly written movie, one far different from what one might expect and from conclusions one might draw from its somewhat misleading trailer, which occasionally makes this film look like the second coming of entries from the Porky's franchise. It's also refreshing to see an offering that isn't afraid to talk about sex in a frank but humorous context without continually turning its story elements into little more than glorified punchlines. And, even though I Want Your Sex is erotically explicit, sensitive viewers take note, it's never depicted gratuitously or in blatantly bad taste. This is all made possible by the film's fine script and sustained pacing, backed by the excellent performances of Wild, What a Year She's Having, Hoffman and the superbly cast ensemble of supporting players, including both those named above and the characters portrayed by Mason Gooding, David Diggs and Chase Sway wonders. It's truly amazing how a picture about a topic that might typically be casually cast aside or summarily denigrated can be as thought-provoking as this one. But, as Erika so often astutely observes, sex can open the door to something that is remarkably revelatory. In our creativity, our actions and our outlooks, and not just in the bedroom.

Elliot, Cooper Hoffman, is working for a renowned artist Erika, Olivia Wilde, when she starts to show a little extra interest in him. He's intrigued and more than a little curious, but he is ill-prepared for just what she has in mind when she invites him back to her home ostensibly for professional purposes and introduces him to her kinky side. Meantime, he's been chucked out of his apartment and is taking a break from his studious and and so is staying with his sexually fluid colleague Zap, Mason Gooding. Now with his sexual boundaries being tested and his eyes, amongst other things, being well and truly opened, his love life becomes something of a rollercoaster to which he is becoming increasingly addicted. The problem might be, though, that Erika isn't exactly reciprocating on any emotional fronts. For her, he has a role and a purpose and she seems quite capable of switching on and off at will much to his chagrin. With his now obvious obsession to her and her power becoming clear, what happens next? The first half hour of this is actually quite groundbreaking, not least because both Hoffman and Wilde throw themselves into their parts enthusiastically and there are some accompanying pithy remarks from the smart-mouthed Zap, but after that it sort of plateaus into something that runs out of steam before becoming vaguely preposterous even by battery-powered standards. Its kinkiness is fun, is cringe-making and is innovative but that isn't sustained and with the dialogue never really making that much of an impact on the proceedings, I'm afraid I sort of lost interest. It certainly emphasizes that pleasures of the flesh and of the mind are not necessarily restricted to people of the opposite sex, nor to anything even remotely conventional But once that point has been made once or twice, I thought this just became a bit repetitious and the conclusion rushed like Agatha Christie on Ketamine. It did worth a look for two initially quite quirky performances, but that's about the height of it.

I had high hopes for this, but boy was I disappointed. Instead of getting Christopher Lee, Boris Karloff or even Arnold Voslo, we get a modern-day Carrie with a few bandages and a rehash of the Azazel story, only this time with a sarcophagus and lots of rusty chains. We begin when the young daughter of Charlie, Jack Rayner, and Larissa, Lea Costa, is abducted by someone at the bottom of their garden who has been grooming her with candy bars at their Cairo home. Despite the best efforts of the police, there proves little that can be done and so the family relocate back to the USA and get on with raising their other two children. Then, out of the blue, Detective Zachy, Mae Callamoy, calls to say she has been found after an aeroplane crashed in the desert. Catatonic, the young girl, Natalie Grace, is brought home but swiftly we realize that all is not well and that when things begin to go bump in the night, some malevolence becomes apparent. What could possibly happen next? Well, sadly, there isn't the slightest hint of jeopardy about any of that as the visual effects designers go into overdrive and the writers head back to the pub. There simply isn't anything here that is remotely scary nor that does any justice to the ancient Egyptian mythology that could have better underpinned this mystery had Lee Cronin actually taken some trouble to build on that richness instead of sticking with the typical family panicky melodrama, albeit entertainingly augmented with some modern-day false teeth. There is the slightest of twists at the denouement that did make me smile until I realized that might also signal sequel and then I left to go home and watch a film that actually evokes something of the eerie and the mystical from this ancient culture. At least she wasn't a doll.

We can all just say that this is Evil Dead, right? I mean, it is, in everything but name, with some flimsy other story tacked on over it. It is shot like Evil Dead, its dialogue fits the Evil Dead, the narrative is Evil Dead. It just happens to not be Evil Dead. And it is all the worse for it. Because it is not Evil Dead, and instead tries to say something else, but gets bogged down in its format and becomes this bland, uninteresting goop. It is proficient, sure, but it is almost desperate, and it is not engaging, and certainly not fun.

Partially entertaining possession flick. Going into it blind, I was expecting more focus on the mummy aspect of things, but that turned out to simply be a surface-level harness around a possession story that is ditched as fast as it appeared. The plot gets lost in itself towards the second half of the movie and it ends up wishy-washing around with classic possession tropes and inevitably ends up falling flat. Overall I was entertained for a good bit, but also bored and annoyed for a significant portion of the movie.

Glumhouse never disappoints. Lee Cronin's The Mummy, 2026, takes a fascinatingly different route by treating the monster mythos as a slow-burn, atmospheric tragedy. Instead of relying on jump scares, the film builds a heavy, suffocating sense of dread around a grieving family whose returned daughter is clearly no longer human, wrapped in a terrifyingly realistic, decaying state. The movie shines brightest through its phenomenal sound design, every raspy breath and dry, rustling movement amplifies the isolation of its modern desert setting. It hits a few bumps in the middle when trying to tie its intimate story back to broader ancient hieroglyphic lore, and anyone hoping for a high-octane adventure will be disappointed. However, as a grim, psychological exploration of an ancient curse infecting a household, it is a beautifully shot, incredibly memorable piece of horror filmmaking.

Interesting concept with not only the giant screen but visuals on the sides for certain scenes. Not sure I'd pay for that upgrade but I have become accustomed to the D-Box seats if only to have some separation from people beside me.

It's so woke, stay away stay away. Just joking, it's not woke at all. The girl power moments are when He-Man was Adam before he became He-Man and fit well with the plot. The crazy cultist actually did a great job as Skeletor, like he actually did a great job. It paid homage to the cartoon. It was colorful, I mean it seriously popped and I appreciate that, it made it look fun and drew me in. It respected the cartoon, it respect the IP, it respected the fans, it really didn't shout politics, it didn't pull a Kevin Smith and insult He-Man for being masculine. In short it was just a fun and entertaining film that was made for the nostalgia seeking fans. However, some of the jokes didn't work, they didn't fit, they felt too MCU, especially in the first half. It was a little too long, especially for what it was, and took forever for the plot to really set in. But who cares, He-Man seems like a prime target for the anti-male, anti-white, anti-straight, anti-everything crowd to target. And IT didn't. It was pretty fun and politics free and I honestly was shocked. I went to hate Watch It. Watch it, it's just entertaining. You don't get lectured. It's refreshingly not woke crap.

We learn quite quickly that the Weedy Adam has only just escaped with his life and the Sword of Power as Skeletor, Jared Leto doing his best impersonation of the deceased Alan Rickman, invaded and seized Castle Grayskull. He, now Nicholas Galatcine, didn't manage to keep hold of the sword for long in his new world, and indeed just ended up in the USA working in HR whilst constantly surfing the internet to track it down before the nasty evil in, Alison Brie, manages to secure it for her menacing boss. Luckily, and somewhat comedically, Adam does manage to find his artifact and then luckily for him his childhood friend Tila, Camila Mendez, shows up just in the nick of time to get him back to Eternia. This is now a decimated world crying out for him to restore the Sorceress and the equilibrium of the kingdom. His chances don't look good. His chief enforcer Duncan, Sir Idris Elba, has succumbed to the bottle and somewhat neutered his battle robots so it's more adept with a mop than a blaster, and what passes for the rebellion is highly suspicious of this floppy-haired and strangely dressed lad. Now he has to prove himself to just about everyone, including himself, and turn into the he-man they need. The snag with this is that it takes us almost an hour to get back to Eternia and so kickstart the fantasy elements of the adventure. Once that does get going, I was reminded more of the Thor franchise than anything with Dolph Lundgren, who does feature momentarily with some sagely advice. Galatcine does enter into the spirit of the thing, and he's buffed up well but even for a T-time film, there simply isn't any menace. Skeletor barely features until the Denuma where there's precisely no jeopardy and we stray perilously closer to soap rather than to peril for me. It looks fine, the visual effects do their job adequately enough, but I really wanted more of He-Man than H.R. Man. Disappointing, sorry.

Travis Knight's reboot easily becomes the highest-rated entry in the franchise's film history, and it earns it. Jared Leto's Skeletor steals the show, balancing humor and villainy in a way that lives up to the memes, and Galatine nails He-Man's heroism and Prince Adam's emotional core. Daniel Pemberton's score embraces the 80s roots with glee. The fun is undeniable, the comedy and action-packed sword-fighting land for critics and audiences alike. It's just 40 minutes too long and leans too hard on self-deprecating meta-humor where sincerity would've hit harder.

This is not a great movie, but that doesn't make it less fun. This is nostalgia bait, and anyone who tells you different has fallen for it. It is well produced, obviously. A lot of money has gone into it. The casting is great, the story does what it needs to. The bad guy is comedically comical. The line deliveries are hokey. All of these things that you expect from a Saturday morning cartoon from the 80s. The music stings remind me more of Flash Gordon than it does He-Man. And that's a shame, because Flash Gordon was a far superior movie in that it was hokey but it took itself seriously. This does not. It tries to be both earnest and self-referential, and it comes off as disingenuous and pandering. It's not a great movie. It's a fun watch, but it is utterly forgettable. And the inclusion of Dolph, while appreciated by the older fans I'm sure, does not mitigate the fact that this movie is just another cash grab.

I expected it to be a children's movie going in so I was already giving it a lot of leeway. I watched it to see if it was something that we'd recommend to our nieces and nephews. There is zero chance that any of us would feel comfortable sitting our nieces down in front of a children's cartoon movie that doesn't seem to realize that sexual innuendo is not appropriate for kids.

What a shame that Travis Knight's Masters of the Universe, at the time of this writing, appears destined to become one of the summer's biggest box office disappointments, struggling to recoup its reported $200 million budget in a crowded theatrical landscape. Perhaps the economics of supply and demand simply caught up with Eternia. After all, another live-action trip back to the heyday of 1980s cartoon serials hardly seemed like something audiences were clamoring for. The dismal reception afforded the 1987 version, whose failure helped hammer the final nail into canon film's coffin, hardly inspired confidence either. Yet Knight's film, working from a screenplay by Chris Butler and brothers Adam and Aaron Nye, swings for the fences in an unexpectedly entertaining blend of fantasy adventure and comedy. Tonally, the gamble pays off. These larger-than-life characters inhabit a world where sincerity and camp are not mutually exclusive, and the film wisely embraces both. Gen Zers, like myself, will appreciate the multiple callbacks to the animated series from over 40 years ago as the film even finds a humorous way to weave in pronouns and a very on-brand Dolph Lundgren cameo for the 21st century. But the biggest question mark entering production was its cast, particularly Jared Leto as Skeletor. Given his recent box office track record, one could be forgiven for expecting the worst. Surprisingly, Leto leans into the character's theatricality and campy absurdity, delivering a performance far better than expected. More impressive, however, is the supporting cast. Idris Elba is perfectly cast as Duncan, better known as Man-at-Arms, bringing warmth, humor, and gravitas to Atternia's chief weapons master. Alison Brie makes for a delightfully cunning Eva Lin, while Maureena Baccarin lends genuine mysticism and dignity to the sorceress. But the film ultimately belongs to Nicholas Galatzine. In his first true starring role, Galatzine finds all the right marks, balancing swashbuckling action with an easygoing comedic charm that makes Prince Adam instantly likeable. More importantly, he understands that He-Man works best when played with conviction rather than irony. No, Masters of the Universe is not the fantasy epic that will dethrone the Lord of the Rings. But as a colorful, earnest, and surprisingly funny adventure, it succeeds far more often than it fails. That makes its disappointing box office performance all the more unfortunate, as this latest trip to Atternia deserved the opportunity to continue its story in a sequel. In an era where studios endlessly mine intellectual property for diminishing returns, it's ironic that one of the few adaptations willing to embrace its own goofy, heroic spirit may never get the chance to build a franchise.

Watching modern cinema try to resurrect 80s franchises has become an exercise in patience and, usually, pure frustration. When a new Masters of the Universe movie was announced, the promise was to bring back the grandeur of that world using today's technology. But instead of honoring the original, the studio delivered an exhausting, soulless adventure that feels ashamed of its own roots. Rather than embracing the colorful, campy fantasy of Eternia, the film constantly hides behind worn-out, self-deprecating irony. It's terrified to take its source material seriously. This heavy reliance on cheap nostalgia and Easter eggs might try to pander to older fans, but it leaves newcomers completely lost, resulting in a movie with a massive identity crisis. Director Travis Knight usually brings a lot of heart to his projects, but he really struggles with an epic of this scale. The direction feels messy, and the shaky camera work during action scenes makes it almost impossible to tell who is fighting who. Add in a heavy reliance on unfinished green screens, and the movie completely loses any sense of physical weight. You don't feel the impact of a sword strike, you just see a blur of digital lights. The script, written by Chris Butler, Aaron Nye, and Adam Nye, only drags things down further. It's a bloated take on the hero's journey that constantly ruins moments of genuine drama with forced, cynical jokes. To make matters worse, the characters don't actually talk to each other, they just deliver robotic, cringy motivational speeches that kill any chance of an emotional connection. Originally, this franchise was all about fun, colorful escapism, a giant barbarian fighting a talking skeleton. But the writers insist on forcing dense social commentary and philosophical dilemmas into a plastic universe that just can't handle them. This completely tanks the pacing, especially in the second act, which is bogged down by pointless political subplots that do nothing for the main story. Honestly, the editors could have easily chopped off 40 minutes without losing anything important, and we would have had a much tighter, far less tedious movie. The cast doesn't help either, as they all seem to be running on autopilot with zero chemistry. Nicholas Galatine tries his best to carry the lead, but Prince Adam is written as so passive and boring that he loses all his classic nobility. We spend way too much time with his angsty human side before He-Man finally shows up, and Galatine looks visibly uncomfortable delivering his artificial lines. Camila Mendes is also totally wasted. Her version of Tila is stripped of her original bravery and reduced to a bitter character with terrible dialogue, only to be completely sidelined as a spectator in the final act. And seeing an actor of Idris Elba's caliber reduced to a glorified extra as Duncan is tough to watch. He's just there to dump exposition and drop tired one-liners instead of acting as a meaningful mentor. Then there's Jared Leto's Skeletor, which is an absolute disaster. He turns the franchise's most iconic villain into a hysterical, theatrical joke with a bizarre voice that totally takes you out of the movie. Because he's so over-the-top and never feels like a credible threat, all the tension in the film completely falls apart. On a technical level, the movie is just as exhausting. The aggressive, guitar-heavy soundtrack never gives you a moment to breathe, often drowning out important dialogue. Visually, instead of a cool mix of sci-fi and medieval fantasy, Eternia looks cheap, sterile, and generic. The costumes look like amateur cosplay, lacking any real grit or wear and tear from a world at war. Everything is so polished and smothered in fake-looking CGI that the big epic battles end up feeling like an outdated video game cutscene, with actors clearly just floating in a green screen room. In the end, Masters of the Universe completely fumbles its chance to be a massive summer blockbuster. Throwing a ton of money at a movie can't buy it a soul. It's frustrating to see a mythology with so much potential reduced to poorly timed jokes and bad CGI because the filmmakers didn't have the guts to just embrace the fantasy. But hey, movies are subjective. What I see as a bloated disaster might be a fun, nostalgic weekend ride for you. If you're curious, grab a ticket and see for yourself, sometimes ripping apart a giant mess of a movie is the best part of the whole experience.

It's bright, breezy, and brimming with heart, even if its jokey tone occasionally undermines the peril. What works, production, performances, and fan service the production, costumes, and sets are first class. Eternia is brought to vibrant, Asgardian-like life, and the world feels lush and authentic. It's a significant step up from the 1987 version, spending most of its runtime in Eternia rather than on Earth. The standout performances elevate the material. Idris Elba is perfectly cast as Duncan slash man-at-arms, bringing courage, wisdom, and dry humour to the mentor role. With multiple post-credit scenes including a mid-credits stinger introducing a mysterious woman with a familiar sword, Adora, aka Chiara, and a final scene teasing Skeletor's return, it's clear they intend to keep the story going. The Verdict Masters of the universe is a fun, colourful, and campy thrill ride that embraces its source material with affection and a knowing wink. While its jokey tone and occasionally clunky execution prevent it from reaching the heights of a masterpiece, its heart, production values, and standout performances make it an 8 out of 10. The multiple post-credit scenes set up a universe with promising potential, and it will be good to see what transpires. Watch if asterisky you're a fan of the classic animated series, enjoy bright and breezy fantasy adventures, or want to see Jared Leto have the time of his life as a wonderfully ridiculous Skeletor. Mayday.transcribe: Check out my full review at https://www.manuals.ben.com slash madea Kenneth Branagh steals the show from Ryan Reynolds in an unapologetically formulaic throwback slash rating. B Mayday knows exactly what it wants to be, a fun, unpretentious 80s throwback carried almost entirely by the chemistry between its two leads. Kenneth Branagh is the real standout, gruff and unexpectedly funny, while Ryan Reynolds keeps his usual instincts nicely in check. The action is sharp and the pacing brisk, but the film takes zero risks, predictable from start to finish, with underdeveloped side characters and a Cold War backdrop that never amounts to much. Still, a solid, entertaining watch.

The return of filmmaking as they used to make it what a rare treat it is to be genuinely surprised by a movie nowadays. And how telling it is of contemporary cinema that stumbling upon a gem like this feels more like a stroke of pure luck than the product of routine industry talent. The year is 1987, at the absolute height of the Cold War. Troy assassin Kelly, Ryan Reynolds, a cocky, reckless US Navy pilot, is shot down over enemy territory during a top-secret reconnaissance mission. Stranded in the brutal Siberian wilderness and hunted by Soviet security operatives, his only hope for survival rests on a completely unexpected ally, Nikolai Kenneth Branagh, a gruff carpenter and former KGB agent who, ironically, harbors a deep, secret love for American pop culture, Bruce Springsteen, and Hollywood movies, talk about a needle in a Soviet haystack. Together, this odd couple must bridge their cultural divide to forge a chaotic alliance and outsmart the Bolshevik army, one just wants to get home, while the other is looking for political asylum. After all, who wouldn't want to live in the America of Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush? Directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley show a real knack for balancing witty humor and high-octane action in Mayday. They write, direct, and deliver one of the most entertaining rides of the year, a fresh, unapologetic comedy that plays like a nostalgic love letter to 80s buddy movies and the iconic Top Gun, which gets plenty of nods throughout the film. There is an undeniable chemistry between the two leads, which, in my book, is mostly thanks to the writer's ability to craft rich characters with actual depth and personality, a concept that sadly feels totally alien in today's cinema. Will we ever learn a thing or two from the Coen brothers? Reynolds brings his signature comic magnetism and fast-talking wit, while Branagh perfectly captures the rugged communist captivated by the American way of life. Watching them play off each other on screen almost takes you back, and I emphasis almost, to the classic screwball comedies of Wilder or Lubitsch.

While technically proficient I cannot recommend this in any way.

Minions_&_Monsters.transcribe: When the Yellow Perils manage to gatecrash a film studio and cause havoc on the set of a film, the director is terrified that his two rotund bosses will want his head. Instead, though, they adore the chaos and commission him to make more films featuring the Minions. Swiftly, they go from rags to riches and are hugely popular until... Sound Silent movies have gone the way of the dodo and now there is to be audio. Yikes, who wants to sit in a drive-in and listen to lots of squeaking and squawking coming from these diminutive stars? Well, nobody really, and so swiftly they are back out on poverty row once more with nowhere to go. James and his pal Henry conclude that their filmmaking days are not yet over when their erstwhile director gives them an old-boxed brownie, but they need a baddie. What better one than a monster? And when they stumble upon an ancient book of spells and arouse the mischievous goomy they appear to have solved their problem without realising that this isn't so much a big jelly of a stage-beasty, it's one that is being controlled to absorb everything in its path be that animal, mineral or solid concrete. Now it is the pretty urgent task of these Minions to reverse their spell before they, and all of their fellows, become extinct. Aside from this being quite an entertaining homage to the golden days of Hollywood it's all just a terribly predictable and dare I say forgettable affair. I enjoyed the Minions best when they were the henchies of the menacing Gru, but here the whole thing just lacks soul a bit and the normally appealing gibberish where we try to pick out actual words in any language from their twittering started to annoy me for the first time as this stretched out what felt like an half-hour television episode into a thinly spread feature. For some reason it's told to us via a reflective narration from a museum curator so there isn't even any jeopardy either and I left thinking it really quite disappointing. Certainly it's a watchable effort and the kids in the cinema did seem to love it, but there's much less for those grown-ups amongst us and it seems to content to rest on its previous laurels a little too much for me.

Moana.transcribe: Check out my full review at https://www.manualsbento.com slash Moana-2026-Stranded- on dash a dash soundstage dash of dash pure dash nostalgia rating. See Moana had every chance to expand on its animated predecessor, and it wastes almost all of it. Beat for beat identical to the 2016 original, this remake trades vibrant, sun-drenched color for green screen sterility, turning musical numbers that once felt joyously alive into stiff, mechanical spectacle. The lead performance brings real warmth to the title role, and the central chemistry has its moments, but neither is enough to disguise a film that never once asks why it needed to exist.

On a gorgeous Polynesian island where they all speak very slowly, the young Moana, Catherine Lagaya, is conflicted by her father's, John Tuay, warning never to venture beyond the reef that protects their home and her grandmother, Rena Owen, who is embedded more in the tribe's ancestral and mystical roots and who has little fear of the open ocean and what lies beyond. When their crops all start to die, she is reminded of the legend of the demigod Maui, Dwayne Johnson, who took the heart stone from the benign goddess from whom all life sprang, and so she determines to find him and his magical hook and then restore the ornate stone to this font of all goodness. Perhaps that will reverse the process that is killing everything? Ten years on from the original animation, and this doesn't really add very much to a story that was always a bit cheesy and thin. Here, it's at least 45 minutes before the film really gets going and Johnson enters the fray, and even then it's all just a little too formulaic. He does look like he's enjoying himself, but Lagaya hasn't much by way of charisma to match and my favorites, the dart-blowing, sea-going, coconut critters, barely feature at all. The two songs that underpin this are familiar enough by now, but the rest of the music is borderline bland and by the rather hastily arrived at conclusion of this perfectly watchable but entirely forgettable rehash. I was wondering if they were already cannibalizing the set from the Lion King on stage ready for the next iteration of Moana, the musical. It's pretty to look at but isn't much more than expensively crafted wallpaper, sorry.

Mortal_Kombat_II.transcribe: Remember the start of Galaxy Quest, 1999, when a group of actors are drafted in to help rescue the universe from a nasty megalomaniac bent on intergalactic domination? Well, this time it's poor old Johnny Cage, Carl Urban, who's the past his sell-by-date thespian reluctantly recruited by Lord Raiden, Tadanobu Asano, to help save the Earth realm from certain doom. He is to join four other somewhat skeptical fighters, all with various skills, to combat the five soldiers of Shao Kahn, Martin Ford, who has been hitherto indestructible as the Princess Kitana, Adeline Rudolph, can attest having seen her father slain when her own kingdom fell. Now adopted and trained by this nemesis, and together with her formidable friend Jade, Tati Gabriel, she looks certain to reduce Johnny and his cohort to dust. Things become even more doom-laden when an all-powerful amulet is accidentally delivered by Aussie rogue Kano, Josh Lawson, into the hands of the Kahn and getting this sorted out is going to take them all to the perilous netherworld for quite a battle royal. Now this is really quite a good fun action adventure if you take it on face value, and it is certainly no worse than than the first of these Simon McAvoyed outings from five years ago, but the dialogue is pretty torrid and even though he looks like his tongue is fixed firmly in his cheek, Urban just hasn't the charisma to pull this off and so he does really rather let this down. That said, along the way there are plenty of homages to other films in this genre. The visual effects are pretty spectacular and there are loads of perfectly choreographed and acrobatically staged combat scenes that are straight out of Kung Fu Panda to keep us entertained as the plot heads in a fairly predicable direction. Not great, no, but it passes two hours easily enough.

Unbearably, tooth-achingly bad. Now, you can only do so much with a plot of a computer game from the early 90s that has been filmed umpteen times already, but this is a new low. And a cleaned up, one-dimensional version of Butcher can't save it. Just no.

On first watch of the trailer, I expected that Johnny Cage would be the centerpiece, capitalizing on Carl Urban's name. While the usual formulaic approach and a bit of convoluted and disjointed script, it did pay homage to the previous film, though not the video game. I did appreciate that they gave mostly equal balance to the different characters, though it lacked backstories to everyone but Cage. We expect the acting to be fun and not deep, except for Cage, which we expected. The special effects were decent, though a few things could have been better. I liked the choice of actors, though Urban is a bit too old for the role, instead of many being young and inexperienced, they went with an older, more seasoned cast which gave the characters more weight. Only the Johnny Cage gave notice to the advanced age. Liu Kang's fire special effects were really overdone, but the rest of the movie was not drowning in special effects. Overall, it was a decent film, with a thin plot, okay acting, but a generally fun time. As for the negative, I would say the disjointed script that didn't really refresh any previous plot points was a bit confusing and took away from the experience. Highlights, I liked the choice of an older cast instead of a bunch of 20-somethings that didn't add gravitas to the characters. Low lights, a couple of SFX misses, confusing subplots, and no resolution for Cage's special abilities. Acting, 5 out of 10 special effects, 5 out of 10 writing, 3 out of 10 directing slash cinematography, 7 out of 10 editing, 6 out of 10 overall entertainment, 6 out of 10.

Obsession.transcribe: Curry Barker has crafted something mostly special for an almost non-existent budget. The story is compelling, the acting is solid, and Obsession feels like a breath of fresh air in comparison to similar horror films. However, it's disappointing that one shrill character trait nearly ruins the entire film. It's because of this that Obsession will have to settle for being a well-made, well-written film dominated by one aggressively irritating character, which will hinder future re-watches much like Frank Darabont's The Mist.

Bear, Michael Johnston, has a crush on his pal Nikki, and Navarette, but it's a love that dare not speak its name. He hasn't the courage to even ask her out. When she decides that she has had enough of their two-horse town and wants to move away, he decides to buy her a gift and a lights-on-a-make-a-wish toy. Make your wish and it will come true as surely as if it were rubbed out on that lamp of Aladdin. Well he gives her a lift home, but their parting is a bit wobbly and so in a fit of peak he snaps the gift and makes his wish after she has gone. What he doesn't expect is that it will come true, but that's just the start as the consequences of his hastily considered prayer begin to take over just about everyone's lives and not necessarily for the better or the safer either. Things don't improve much for him when he discovers that his options to reverse his heart's desire are limited in the extreme. It's a toss-up between the pair at the top of the billing here, but I reckon Navarette might just have edged it on the acting front as both deliver positively visceral performances with this horror as it takes on a whole new perspective of maniacally temperamental behaviour and turns any sense of romance into something positively hysterical, menacing and at times quite menacingly gory and funny too. I really did enjoy the Denouement and I reckon this is the best I've seen from this genre in 2026 so far. Never mind careless talk, just beware what you wish for?

Full review, Alzit Reviews.com waking up in the middle of the night with the eerie sense that you're being watched, only to look down and see your kid standing pitch black next to your bed staring at you. That is the exact level of visceral dread this movie locks you into. Obsession is one of those rare, deeply unsettling horror films that doesn't just want to jump-scare you, it actively wants to get under your skin and suffocate you. You get about 15 minutes of relative safety at the start, but the exact second that one wish willow snaps, the air is completely sucked out of the room. You could literally hear a collective wave of tension ripple through the theatre. Ind Navarette is phenomenal. Her ability to instantly pivot from an obsessed, psychotic girlfriend back to a normal, completely terrified Nikki who realizes she's trapped and then snap right back into the madness is chilling. The bedroom scene where she watches Bear Sleep is going to stick with me for a long time. Massive props to director Curry Barker for making a flawless leap from YouTube horror to the big screen. He relies on old-school atmosphere rather than cheap audio cues, masterfully weaponizing camera placement, shadows, and lingering silence. There is a shot of her just standing there smiling that goes on for so long it made the entire crowd audibly uneasy. With all the respect in the world, this is a one-timer for me because I am in no rush to put myself back through this emotional meat grinder. But it is an absolute must experience with a theatre crowd. Verdict, front row, an absolute must see.

Curry Barker's feature debut is a flawless, deeply unsettling masterpiece that takes the classic be careful what you wish for trope and turns it into a relentless nightmare. The film centers on a music store employee who uses a supernatural trinket to force his longtime crush to love him, unleashing a wave of horrifying, unhinged consequences. Visually striking and meticulously paced, the movie keeps you completely locked in from the opening frame to its devastating conclusion. What elevates this psychological horror film to absolute perfection are the phenomenal acting performances from Michael Johnston and Ind Navarette. Johnston is brilliant as bear, capturing a desperate, tragic vulnerability that makes his downward spiral incredibly painful to watch. Navarette delivers a tour de force performance as Nicky, flawlessly shifting between heartbreaking torment and a chilling, vacant fixation that anchors the entire film. It is an intense, unforgettable ride that stands out as one of the absolute best entries in modern horror.

Writer, director Curry Barker's leap from YouTube viral fame to the big screen is one of the best success stories in Hollywood, and Kane Parsons' backrooms for a 24 later this month appears to be further proof that the road from YouTube to Hollywood, while still less traveled, can make all the difference. The viral success of Barker's **milk and cereal** 2024, https://letterboxd.com//fixitnbinge//film//milk-cereal, showcased enormous potential and a natural instinct for low-budget horror filmmaking, making his transition to the big screen feel like a well-earned graduation. In Obsession, Barker has crafted a slow-burn psychological horror film that steadily builds Kareen's towards its shocking conclusion. While the deliberate pacing occasionally tested my patience, once Barker's story fully unfolds, it seeps into the viewer's psyche in ways few recent horror films have managed, provoking deeply uncomfortable questions about consent and free agency, while possibly making you think twice before blowing out candles on your next birthday. Obsession presents a seemingly innocuous setup centered on the lovelorn bear, Michael Johnston, who literally wishes to escape the friend zone with his longtime pal Nicky and Navarette. After stumbling upon a one-wish Willow collector's item in a New Age Curio shop, one that wouldn't feel out of place beside the Zolter machine in the Tom Hanks smash hit Big, 1988, Bear makes a wish without understanding the terrifying power he has unleashed. Encouraged by his best friend Ian, frequent Barker collaborator Cooper Tomlinson, Bear initially appears to get everything he wants when Nicky suddenly develops a romantic interest in him. But soon the wheels start to come off as Bear's happily ever after spirals into a nightmare after the possessiveness of Nicky becomes increasingly unhinged. Navarette delivers a terrifying performance that has echoes of fatal attraction and single, white, female with additional layers of psychological torture for her loss of bodily autonomy with shocking moments of terror, expertly sustained tension, disturbing imagery and a fearless performance from Navarette, Obsession stands as one of the year's best horror films.

There's a fine line between genuine affection and possession, and horror movies usually thrive when crossing it. I went into obsession expecting a psychological deep dive into emotional dependency, but what we actually get is an experience that violently swings between brilliance and frustration. Directed by Curry Barker, the film swings big in its attempt to show toxic masculinity and the loss of free will. The first 30 minutes are genuinely suffocating, doing a great job of making you feel trapped. But while Barker takes huge risks for his debut feature, the movie stumbles trying to keep that momentum going. The real trouble starts when the story needs to stretch past its initial premise. The second act drags hard, trapping the viewer in a repetitive loop of jealousy and chasing that goes nowhere. They could have easily chopped at least 20 minutes in the editing room. On top of that, the indie budget really shows, scenes meant to be psychologically oppressive are ruined by amateurish lighting and set designs that break the immersion. Worse still is the jarring mix of tones. Right when the discomfort peaks, the script throws in bizarre dark humor. A badly timed joke or a goofy reaction completely kills the dramatic weight, making it clear the director hasn't quite learned how to trim the fat from his own ideas. The whole plot with the mystical artifact hooks you at first, but it loses steam once the curse actually kicks in. Instead of building tension, the narrative just stalls. This makes the interactions suffer, too. Dedicated actors are stuck delivering stiff, unnatural dialogue, forced to spell out feelings that their body language was already showing perfectly. It makes some of the more dramatic scenes feel like a bad teen soap opera draft. Following the protagonist, Bear, Michael Johnston, for almost two hours is a tough pill to swallow. He's a pathetic guy whose harmless neediness quickly turns into a sick, one-dimensional selfishness. While the movie doesn't shy away from exposing the ugliest sides of possessiveness disguised as romance, Bear has zero redeeming qualities, making the watch tedious since there's no one to root for. If the movie survives its structural flaws, it's almost entirely thanks to Ind Navarette. Tasked with playing a character who gets psychologically beaten down by both the male lead and bad writing, she delivers an incredibly mature, visceral performance. Her subtle shifts in posture and gaze anchor the whole movie, making her the only real emotional core in the story. Using folk horror to talk about toxic masculinity is the coolest idea here, but the execution completely lacks subtlety. The movie talks down to the audience, hammering its message home so hard that it feels more like a lecture than an organic psychological study. This also exposes a major flaw in how it handles its female lead. In trying to call out abuse, the narrative reduces her to a mere tool for suffering, tortured just to push the bad guy's arc forward. It leaves you wondering if it's genuinely critiquing misogyny or just exploiting women's trauma for shock value. The film's early strength is its grounded tension, relying on everyday paranoia rather than monsters in the dark. But by the third act, the director throws all that out the window and goes full grotesque. Instead of feeling earned, this sudden bloodbath of graphic violence feels like a desperate crutch to shock an already bored audience. The sound design also fumbles, they went for an eerie lack of music, which works at first, but ends up making long scenes feel empty. When loud noises do happen, they're poorly mixed and feel like cheap jump scares. After racing through a chaotic, blood-soaked climax, the movie just ends. An abrupt cut to black rolls the credits without explaining the artifact or the rules of the curse. It doesn't feel like a thought-provoking open ending, it just feels like the writers painted themselves into a corner and didn't know how to wrap things up, leaving you waiting for a payoff that never comes. In the end, obsession is a tough, uneven watch. Curry Barker has the guts to poke at the painful wounds of toxic relationships, and End Navarette's amazing acting keeps things afloat. But the pacing issues, weird tonal shifts, and the rushed, gory climax really test your patience. Still, it forces you to think. Horror is supposed to push us out of our comfort zone, right? If you want to feel that oppressive atmosphere, it's worth a watch. Just go in with a strong stomach, ready for the messy pacing, and see how you handle the sudden silence when those credits finally roll.

Emotional hijacking Bear is a shy, introverted young man working in a music shop who is deeply and secretly in love with his friend and colleague, Nikki. Desperate over his unrequited romantic longing, Bear acquires a mysterious supernatural object called the Weeping Willow, which has the power to grant wishes. Blind to the consequences, he wishes for Nikki to fall in love with him more than anything else in this world. The spell works instantly, but the idyllic dream swiftly morphs into a nightmare, Nikki's implanted love mutates into an irrational, suffocating, and deeply disturbing behavior. Her morbid devotion erases the boundaries of her sanity, unleashing a downward spiral of violence and obsessive possessiveness that threatens to destroy both their lives and everyone around them. In certain aspects, obsession stands out as the great revelation of contemporary horror cinema. Operating on a shoestring budget of just $750,000, director Curry Barker achieves what many Hollywood blockbusters can only dream of, building an atmosphere of tension relying strictly on the power of ideas, a fresh approach to staging and raw storytelling. Barker taps into 1980s cinematic references, taking the classic premise of magical manipulation, W.W. Jacob's The Monkey's Paw, and transplanting it into deeply uncomfortable psychological territory. The horror becomes visceral, psychological, and existential, confronting us with the terrifying facets of the human ego. It seeks to prove that forcing someone to love you does not stem from devotion, but rather from a craving for control and a pathological fear of loneliness or rejection. Finally, a humble piece of advice for a talented Curry Barker, who will never read this review but is still in the budding stages of his career, the over-reliance on jump-scare audio stingers is symptomatic of an endemic disease, one that blends narrative laziness, behavioral psychology, and the familiar commercial pressures of Hollywood. Do not fall into the temptation of mimicking the cheapest tropes of late-career Shyamalan. Instead, fully exploit that aesthetic and cinematic creativity currently flourishing within you. Flee once and for all from cheap, gimmicky cords, and lose your fear of silence. Remember that true horror dwells in the stillness of masterpieces like Nesferatu, Les Diaboliques or Rosemary's Baby, by Murnau, Clusso, and Polanski, respectively.

Even the addition of Dan Stevens in a supporting role as septuagenarian Hans Kimmler, a character who appears to be an amalgamation of Joseph Menjel and Dr. Strangelove, fails to land. In fact, given the character's parodic underpinnings, he might have worked better in a comedy. The set-up seems oddly familiar, genetically engineered super soldiers escape a nearby military bunker and go on a pointless killing spree, murdering everything that moves in their path. It's 1992's sci-fi actioner Universal Soldier, except without the charm of Van Damme or the psychotic menace of Dolph Lundgren. Corritten with Simon Barrett, Wingard's film appears to have fallen prey to an overzealous final cut that strips away some necessary exposition. Why exactly does Rebecca Hall's character inexplicably have literal blood on her hands during one interstitial telephone scene that comes with zero set-up? MMA fans who recognized Alex Pouetin-Parrera in the opening credits are likely to be equally underwhelmed, with his zero dialogue and brooding stares amounting to little more than physical presence as one of three super soldiers who bring an orgy of death to a small New Mexico desert town. Seemingly caught in their path of destruction is a run-down trailer park managed by single mom and military vet Celeste, played by Audria Arjona. As the super soldiers turn the mobile home park into Swiss cheese for the crime of simply being in their way, Celeste, with the help of Reginald Veljonsson's Josiah, fights back. Wingard and Barrett seem more committed to developing Arjona's character at the expense of more interesting characters such as Stevens Kimmler and his wife, Hannah Kimmler, Hall, which is a shame, as the film ends with an end title sequence suggesting a follow-up could be in the works. Heaven help us. A flimsy plot, a paint-by-numbers action set-up, and, dare I say it, the wasting of Arjona's considerable talent make Onslaught a muddled, lifeless mess that proves all the blood, bullets and body count in the world can't resurrect a movie with no pulse.

PAW_Patrol_The_Dino_Movie.transcribe: Paw Patrol, the Dino movie continues the franchise's streak of fun, action-packed movies about one boy and a team of puppies rescuing people from danger by transporting our furry little friends from the mean streets of Adventure City to an island full of dinosaurs. The visuals, humor, action, and storyline all vibed with me perfectly, with my favorite thing being that Marshall's backstory wasn't about a traumatic reason for him being clumsy, but instead he chose to continue pursuing his goals despite his clumsiness. That's a refreshing take on the clumsy person trope as it shows clumsiness is a choice, not a medical condition that needs to be treated. Keeping Adventure City briefly shown in the opening but still visible ensures continuity between movies, even though it is a little bit sad that Liberty is absent. Having Mayor Humdinger return as the movie's antagonist but actually start out wanting a new, honest life shows a level of growth and accountability that the series previously never used. Before, Humdinger felt like a one-dimensional caricature of a politician with sneaky, conniving motives, but now, he actually feels like a new man, and him relapsing due to the diamonds on the Dinosaur Island, Dino Island as it is called, is very in-character and shows that growth is not a one-way street. The voice cast particularly McKenna Grace as Skye, Jennifer Hudson as Lillian Ledds, and Terry Crews as Alistair Stonewall were outstanding and delivered some funny, delightful performances. I also really loved the new songs Bottle Up by Backstreet Boys and Work by Ava Max. Not only do these songs feel like modern bangers any kid would listen to, but they also fit the story's themes very well, with Bottle Up serving as a literal expression of how the Paw Patrol is bottling up their emotions in being awestruck by an entire island full of dinosaurs, while Work highlights how they have to save the island from being destroyed by a volcano Humdinger activates with a mound of dynamite. My only criticism and something I've always had with the Paw Patrol franchise's movies is how fast-paced the movie is. Because the movies prioritize the preschool-age audience, they forget that longer pacing can allow for better world-building and stronger character growth. Kid-friendly studios in animation like Dreamworks or Pixar have done this for years and it shows. But overall, Paw Patrol, the Dino movie was a fun, action-packed ride that continued to wow me with a visually spectacular story about resilience and doing the hardest things even when you have a flaw that seemingly holds you back. I hope we get more of these movies in the next three to four years or so.

Primetime.transcribe: A true crime story this inherently bizarre should not require much embellishment, yet primetime spends so much energy dressing itself up that the actual story gets buried underneath the filmmaking. What could have been a sharp, uncomfortable examination of television, celebrity, and the ethics of true crime instead becomes a frustratingly uneven film that mistakes stylistic excess for substance. Robert Pattinson gives a pretty good performance as Chris Hansen, bringing enough conviction to make the central figure compelling even when the screenplay does not. The supporting cast is strong as well. Skyler Giussondo makes an impression as the adult decoy pretending to be an underage boy, while Merritt Weaver brings welcome dimension as the show's producer. There are also genuinely interesting ideas scattered throughout the film, particularly in its examination of how media can commoditize real humans suffering into entertainment. The problem is that primetime rarely develops its ideas into a cohesive story. It often feels less like a narrative and more like a collection of scenes placed next to one another. The result makes it difficult for viewers to become invested in what is happening or, more importantly, in the characters involved. Its aesthetic ambitions are particularly exhausting. The fuzzy mid-2000s look is clearly deliberate, and there is nothing wrong with leaning into the visual language of the period. Here, though, the music, lighting, camera angles, and visual flourishes are pushed so aggressively that the movie starts announcing its artistry rather than letting it emerge naturally. There is a compelling story underneath all the smoke and mirrors, which makes the constant insistence on style feel less like enrichment and more like distraction. The heavier issue is how much the film dramatizes real events and real people. Taking real names and identities while taking substantial creative liberties creates an uncomfortable disconnect, particularly in the portrayal of Hanson himself. The film's portrayal of real-life subjects can make some of its choices feel less like artistic interpretation and more like borderline defamation. Hanson himself has publicly criticized the film, which only makes the question of how responsibly it treats people difficult to ignore. You see how this looks, right? There are also moments where the dramatization crosses into genuinely uncomfortable territory. The film's treatment of SA and mental health issues can feel glib and insensitive. For example, the portrayal of the true story of a man who unalived himself while caught in the to-catch-a-predator investigations is difficult to digest. That was a real human being who faced a genuinely tragic ending, not merely a fictional plot device, and the lack of respect taken toward a serious subject matter invites questions that the movie does not seem particularly interested in answering. Additionally, the creative choice to make the main decoy exclusively male feels conspicuously constructed. The primarily male-on-male encounters feel unrealistic, existing solely to insert the male decoy into the story as a main character. That is unfortunate because Beneath the Excess is a worthwhile film trying to get out. Primetime has something meaningful to say about the ethics of true crime entertainment, the machinery of television, and the uncomfortable relationship between public spectacle and private suffering. But its lack of nuance turns complicated questions into an overly tidy division between good guys and bad guys. The satire gets lost in the dramatization, and the film's strongest observations are repeatedly smothered by its need to make everything bigger, darker, and more cinematic. Ultimately, Primetime is a case of flash-over substance. Pattinson and the supporting cast do solid work, and there are enough provocative ideas here to make the film worth discussing, but the execution repeatedly gets in its own way. When the real story is already compelling, inventing so much around it feels unnecessary, and, in some cases, ethically questionable.

It's been said that we often become what we concentrate upon. That's ironic, because frequently this results in the creation of that which we're purposely trying to avoid. And, in this third feature outing from director Lance Oppenheim, that's precisely what happens to its high-profile protagonist, investigative journalist Chris Hansen, Robert Pattinson. In this fact-based satire, the film follows the ascendancy of the reporter on the tabloid series Dateline NBC, specifically through his work on the shows to catch a Predator segment, 2004 to 2007, in which he covered stories designed to expose the exploits of pedophiles. Working in conjunction with the website-perverted Justice, Hansen, his producer, Merritt Weaver, and a pair of Predator-bait decoy actors, Skyler Giussondo, Phoebe Bridgers, orchestrated sting operations aimed at capturing their unsuspecting prey in the act on camera. While it's undeniable that the intentions with this mission were fundamentally noble, their on-air depictions increasingly took on a vibe of sensationalism, blurring the line between journalism and entertainment. And, as Hansen's star rose, he relished the personal notoriety and ratings popularity that came with his efforts. However, as the film postulates, his increasingly aggressive reporting tactics and quest for professional glory suggest that he was becoming as much of a Predator on the alleged perpetrators as they were on their would-be victims. It might even be said that the methods employed verged on a form of entrapment, an approach that carried significantly murky and curiously ironic consequences. Now, this is not to suggest that Hansen was becoming a sexual Predator himself, but, in donning the cloak of self-appointed activist, his personal authenticity was called into question as he became the target of undercover surveillance for a supposed extramarital affair that was threatened to be exposed by the national inquirer. If the foregoing combination of elements sounds like the makings of a cinematic tall tale, you might indeed be correct. Circumstances like those depicted in the film naturally raise questions about the picture's factual accuracy, Hansen himself has publicly and vocally proclaimed that Primetme paints him in an unfairly erroneous light. Moreover, on this basis, this is a picture that won't appeal to everyone and will likely inspire more than its share of heated debate. However, the purposeful over-the-top approach used here is designed for dramatic effect to reflect the aforementioned question about the blurred lines between journalism and entertainment and the loaded theme of Predator chasing Predator. And, in doing so, the narrative is not meant to be taken as literal truth as much as it is to be looked upon as a metaphor, a satirical psychological thriller using real-life events and characters as the basis for illustrating its particular viewpoints. This becomes especially apparent through this offering's insightful script, which deftly fuses wry humour, incisive camp and tense drama to tell its story, quite a riding feat to pull off successfully. In addition, the picture's superb performances, especially by Pattinson, Giussondo and Bridgers, inventive cinematography and editing, and outstanding original score enhance the story and its various components, combining in a singularly distinctive way suitable for a production with as many diverse elements as are present here. Although this release has a tendency to meander at times, it generally remains faithful to its intents in telling a story with messages and ramifications that go beyond the individual events that make it up, important considerations for all of us to keep in mind in our efforts to create that which we seek and to meticulously avoid that which we don't.
