Going back to a classic is always a slippery slope. When I sat down to watch the highly anticipated sequel to The Devil Wears Prada, I was worried it would just be a pale copy of the original. Unfortunately, the new movie tries so hard to balance the comfort of nostalgia with the decline of print media that it ends up with a bit of an identity crisis. The direction feels strangely bureaucratic, as if the person behind the camera was just checking boxes for an engagement algorithm instead of bringing a unique vision. This is incredibly obvious in the visuals, too. The gritty, frantic warmth of early 2000s New York is gone, replaced by a sterile, overly polished digital look. The luxurious sets that used to feel seductive and oppressive now just feel cold, making the film look more like a generic streaming movie than a pop culture trendsetter. The script basically falls into the soft reboot trap. It recycles the exact same narrative beats and conflicts from the first movie, completely ignoring that these characters are in entirely different stages of their lives. Dealing with the brutal transition to the digital age and the collapse of the print market was the perfect natural path to take, but the execution is incredibly shallow. AI and social media are handled in a way that feels almost cartoonish, like an out-of-touch older executive trying to explain how the internet works. To make matters worse, the pacing really drags in the second act. The story gets bogged down by boring contract negotiations and forced romantic subplots that have zero chemistry and kill any sense of urgency. Everything is wrapped up way too easily in the end, making the whole thing feel like a very safe, predictable rough draft. Bringing Meryl Streep and Hathaway and Emily Blunt back together seemed like a surefire hit, but the reality on screen is pretty disappointing. The undeniable spark from the original is just gone, and their interactions feel so cold and rehearsed that it almost seems like they filmed their scenes in separate rooms. The script's biggest mistake was trying to awkwardly humanize Miranda Priestly. The ruthless, terrifying editor we love to hate has been watered down into a tired, vulnerable executive, which completely strips her commands of their weight and ruins the tension. Emily Blunt's immense talent is also totally wasted. While Andy has clearly matured, Emily is stuck in time, acting as a recycled punching bag who just repeats her bitter complaints from two decades ago without any real character growth. Throw in a new generation of assistants who lack any real charm, and it's clear the brilliant chemistry of the original was left in the past. Ultimately, the movie struggles to find its tone, awkwardly bouncing between 2000's dark comedy and a melancholic drama about the publishing world. It's a victim of its own legacy, playing it too safe and prioritizing commercial demand over any genuine creative vision. But hey, my take shouldn't be the final word. If you're just looking for a cozy hit of nostalgia and aren't too worried about a flawless plot, seeing these familiar faces again might hit you completely differently. I definitely recommend watching it and drawing your own conclusions, your personal connection to the classic might help you look past these flaws and enjoy the return to runway in a way my critical I just couldn't.

The_Dog_Stars.transcribe: Life in a post-apocalyptic world is a common theme in movies, especially, if you believe what's published in the media, the increasing prospect that such an outcome may be coming closer to a reality than any of us might like. In many cases, these films follow the experiences of a resourceful, innovative protagonist who quietly but skillfully struggles to survive, successfully managing to fend off foes while cerebrally wrestling with feelings about what's been lost. That scenario is apparent once again in this latest release from legendary director Ridley Scott. Unfortunately, however, this is not one of the filmmakers' better efforts, a blatantly uneven production that gets things right in some regards but woefully misses the mark in others. Based on the 2012 novel of the same name by Peter Heller, the film follows the life of a mechanic and antique Cessna pilot, H.I.G., Jacob Elordi, who ekes out a comparatively comfortable existence in the Colorado wilderness with his wisecracking marksman wingman, Bangalie, Josh Brolin, in a dystopian future that has been devastated by a deadly virus. Like H.I.G. and Bangalie, pockets of survivalists resistant to the pandemic's lethal impact are scattered across the countryside, but they face constant danger from the encroachment of ruthless scavengers seeking to pilfer whatever they can find for themselves. But, despite the undeniable harshness of this new reality, H.I.G. still pines for a way of life that once was. And he's convinced of rediscovering that possibility when he receives radio messages from a mystery woman, Allison Janney, in Grand Junction, Colorado that ambiguously hold out hope for the existence of such a sanctuary. In his quest to find the truth, he embarks on an adventure-filled journey in which he encounters a variety of other survivors, such as Aaron, Bendict Wong, head of a surprisingly thriving Mennonite community, and a hard-nosed gun-toting rancher, Jack, aka Pops, Guy Pearce, living in a remote and vulnerable locale with his daughter, Seema, Margaret Qualley. But can H.I.G. survive the journey? And what might he find if he ever makes it to Grand Junction? While the premise here is solid, recalling such offerings as I Am Legend, 2007, and films in the Mad Max franchise, the finished product nevertheless occasionally teeters on shaky ground. After a strong but sometimes slow opening hour, backed by a reasonably commendable closing act, in-between viewers are mercilessly subjected to a middle segment that seriously defies believability, taking the picture decidedly off the rails, a serious blow to the film's overall credibility. This is truly regrettable, as this disproportionately out-of-place sequence makes it easy for viewers to quickly lose interest as the project struggles to get back on track before the credits roll. It's difficult to fathom what the filmmaker was going for in such a ridiculously over-the-top sequence, and it detracts from the elements that truly work well, a terrific cast, gorgeous cinematography, and an emotive soundtrack reminiscent of Scott's earlier cinematic opus, Thelma and Amp, Louise, 1991. I can't help but think that this was a case of failure to kill one's darlings, and, in this instance, that shortcoming nearly undermines all of the audience goodwill the picture amasses before and after it. What's more, the script is short on its backstory elements, leaving one wondering how the narrative ultimately arrived at where it is. Sadly, The Dog Stars could have been much better, both as a cautionary tale and as a fine work of big-screen drama, with some deliberate tweaking. As it stands now, though, the survival considerations addressed here could be just as applicable to viewing audiences as they are to the characters themselves.

C Plus The Dog Stars is a gorgeous, contemplative post-apocalyptic thriller that never fully earns its two-hour runtime. Ridley Scott finds real tenderness in a story about grief, isolation, and the fragile work of learning to hope again, and the ensemble cast cells that journey beautifully. In a world where a flu virus has wiped out most of the human population, mechanic-cumpilot HIG, Jacob Elordi, lives on a remote farm with his world-weary pal Bangalie, Josh Brolin. He makes occasional sorties with his beloved dog Jasper into town, think Omega Man 1971, for supplies and to reminisce at the home he shared with his late wife and unborn Berne but is spotted from the ground as he returns home one day and a violent tragedy ensues. That galvanizes him to set off in his plane to find the town of Grand Rapids from where he has had intermittent radio contact over the years. It's at the extreme edge of his range though, and so it's no great surprise when his aircraft blows a gasket and he finds himself crash-landed in a field. Luckily, that just happens to be adjacent to the home SEMA, Margaret Qualley, shares with her curmudgeonly dad, Guy Pearce, who promptly gives him his marching orders. That'll be easier said than done as the field has to be cleared of trees and rubble before he can take off, plenty of time for everyone to get to know each other. Pretty swiftly, the question is more about whether he's going to stay or she's going to go, a decision that is made for them and so it's Grand Rapids here we come. What might they find if, when they get there? There is plenty of attractive aerial photography of the alpine scenery and Brolin does try to bring a little gritty substance to the proceedings as the marauding reapers attempt to raid his only functioning fridge in a 50-square-mile radius. But there isn't anywhere enough by way of action to sustain this couple of hours and the episodic storytelling strays into all too familiar territory very quickly once a lordy sets off on his adventure. Surprisingly for a Scott film, the continuity isn't the best either, the plane is spattered in blood then it isn't, it's attacked by an axe then well it wasn't and the radio aerials are there one minute and not the next, too. That all rather sums up the lackluster nature of this ponderous opportunity for the charismatic but unchallenged a lordy to travel the lengths of the country in his tiny Cessna hopping from frying pan to fire. It's all perfectly watchable but there's very little soul to the thing and with each character bogged down with pre-disease baggage it's a bit like swimming through glue at times, too.

The_End_of_Oak_Street.transcribe: When it comes to summertime movies, many viewers expect fun thrill rides, Escapist fare at its best. At the same time, though, as the summer movie season winds down, expectations tend to lower by the time August rolls around, when the dregs of its remaining releases are unceremoniously rolled out. But, every so often, audiences are in for an unexpected nifty little treat when a sleeper offering hits theaters. Such is the case with the latest effort from writer-director David Robert Mitchell, a Spielbergian sci-fi retro thriller that skillfully drops elements of the Jurassic Park franchise into 1980s suburbia. And it does so with a deft mix of heart-pounding action adventure and raucous, often campy humor. The film follows the adventures of the Platt family, mother Denise and Hathaway, father Greg Ewan McGregor, and teenage children Audrey, Maisie Stella, and Brian, Christian Convery, along with their mischievous but resourceful pooch, an Australian cattle dog named Starbuck. On the surface, everything seems fine, though, as soon becomes apparent, there are some simmering troubles in family household, marital discord, financial difficulties, potential problem drinking, the dashed dreams of adolescence. However, after a bright, intense light appears during a thunderstorm one night, the Platt's world gets turned upside down as their neighborhood experiences a series of infrastructure collapses, along with the appearance of anomalous plant life, specimens that appear to belong to extinct prehistoric species. But that's only the beginning, as these developments are followed by the presence of dinosaurs. Needless to say, the residents of Oak Street are stunned at what they find, and it's not long before survival and escape become imminent concerns. But how? What's more, how did all of this come about? Those are the questions the family and their neighbors face as their world crumbles around them. Admittedly, the premise of this story is a relatively simple one, and it occasionally turns repetitive and derivative as it plays out. However, these shortcomings are made up for by great action sequences and raucously funny laughs, many of them deliberately over-the-top and characterized by ample but restrained gratuitousness, though squeamish viewers may still wish to bow out. A number of typical Spielbergian tropes are also included here, such as the curmudgeonly neighbor, P.J. Byrne, the kindly old lady down the street, and Gee Bird, the mild-mannered but unexpectedly tough, gun-toting midlifer, Emily Corota, the neighborhood bully, Hudson Meek, and the beautiful new neighbor girl, Jordan Alexa Davis, all of whose story threads figure into the flow of the narrative and are sufficiently wrapped up by the time the credits roll. But perhaps the biggest surprise here is the film's integration of subtle but effective themes one might not anticipate from a production like this, such as messages related to second chances, redemption, and forgiveness, which are skillfully incorporated without beating viewers over the head, credit the expertly penned script for this. Thankfully, while many critics acknowledge that there are numerous respectful nods to the Jurassic franchise, most astutely appreciate the big nostalgic fun in this, despite a cantankerously vocal minority of cynical peers who contend such attributes are out-and-out ripoffs of classic cinematic content. I suppose one could see things that way, but that spoils the fun, begging the question about the half-empty-slash-half-full-glass metaphor, one that ultimately comes down to your view-slash-your choice. So what's it going to be? Given the dearth of good, entertaining pictures at this time of year, in my view, the end of Oak Street is genuinely a welcome breath of fresh air in an otherwise stale room, a late summer release that's truly dynamite.

The end of Oak Street is yet another fossilized production from an entertainment industry out of fresh ideas. This is essentially Jurassic Park in 1980s US suburbia. The lead-in is overlong, rather boring, more than a little cliched, leaning heavily on 80s nostalgia to carry it. Beyond that, it's predictable dinosaur action hijinks, a basic family adventure, with a dash of time travel nonsense. Very limited upsides include okay but hardly sterling acting and reasonable special effects. In summary, in this reviewers estimation this flick is what you churn out when you have no fresh ideas. A wholly bland watch that won't challenge the synapses.

A great premise that never quite lives up to its potential The End of Oak Street has one of those premises that immediately sells you on the movie, an ordinary suburban neighborhood suddenly finds itself surrounded by prehistoric wilderness and dinosaurs. Unfortunately, the movie itself never becomes quite as interesting as that setup. There's definitely fun to be had here. The dinosaur sequences are entertaining, and Hathaway and Ewan McGregor are good, and the movie moves along quickly enough that it never really becomes boring. I also appreciated that it feels more like an old-fashioned adventure movie than another attempt to build a giant franchise. The problem is that it spends a surprising amount of time on fairly generic family drama when there's a much more interesting story happening outside the house. The characters never become compelling enough to justify how much attention is given to and some of the emotional moments feel forced rather than earned. It also wears its Spielberg influences very heavily on its sleeve. There's nothing wrong with trying to capture that 1980s Amblin feeling, but at times it feels less inspired by those movies than like it's deliberately trying to recreate them. Still, dinosaurs attacking suburbia is a pretty difficult concept to make completely boring, and there are enough good sequences here to make it worth watching. I just wish the movie had embraced the weirdness of its premise a little more. 6 out of 10.

The Furious delivers a solid, adrenaline-fueled experience that focuses almost entirely on its high-stakes action sequences. The fight choreography is impressive, showcasing sharp, impactful movements that feel heavy and dangerous, largely thanks to the chemistry between Siam Yao and Joe Taslim. However, the film struggles when it tries to slow down, as the narrative is quite thin and the dialogue often feels like an afterthought. While it lacks the thematic depth or character development to make a lasting impact, it succeeds as a straightforward, brutal display of martial arts skill. If you are looking for a visually driven, no-nonsense action flick that prioritizes physicality over storytelling, it delivers exactly what it promises.

Bone-crushingly brutal, stunt and fight coordinator turned director Kenji Tanigaki's The Furious is the martial arts action film you've been waiting for. When it comes to all-out martial arts films of this caliber, plot and character typically take a backseat to the spectacle of violence but in Tanigaki's The Furious, the story satisfyingly achieves parody with the gut-wrenching action. Single father Wang Wei, Miao Xia, spends time with his young daughter Rainie and Yeo Yang as a working-class handyman on the outskirts of their city when human traffickers snatch her off the streets, setting in motion a sequence of events that will test his endurance like nothing before. As Wang Wei desperately tears apart and bludgeons his way through the criminal underworld looking for his daughter he crosses paths with Navim, Joe Taslim, who is also combing through the same clues in search of his missing wife. Set within a fictional Southeast Asian landscape that seamlessly blends Thai, Indonesian, Chinese, and Japanese influences, The Furious creates a distinctive sense of place that enriches every frame. Once Wang Wei and Navim team up together in a pairing as satisfying as 2022's RRR, the action goes full throttle in an unrelenting orgy of broken bones, crushed skulls, and violence, showcasing martial arts disciplines ranging from Chinese wushu and kung fu to judo and penchak silat. Speaking of penchak silat, the inclusion of Yeo Yang Ruyin, whose discipline is penchak silat, as a ruthless, bow-and-arrow assassin is just icing on the cake. Every fighting sequence involving Ruyin is a masterclass in viciousness that will slake the bloodlust of the most die-hard martial arts fan. With a surprising third act that escalates the action and tension, The Furious avoids the pitfall so many martial arts films tend to make with formulaic, predictable endings taking twists and turns that will leave a bittersweet taste. Hands down the best action film of the year, Tanagaki's The Furious will satisfy fans of the raid films, and now belongs in the conversation as one of the finest martial arts action films in the 21st century. Brian Lu Wu Ji Ji Yanen, Sahajak Bunthiniket, and Minatsunen Fengler Duansikul co-star.

When action movies drop the deep philosophical stuff and just focus on raw human mechanics, the result is usually hit or miss, but The Furious definitely hits the mark. Directed by Kenji Tanigaki, the film is a brutal, primal survival trip that uses physical force and instinct to do all the talking. Instead of trying to reinvent the classic revenge story, the movie leans hard into the pure spectacle of movement. The fight scenes feel like a highly destructive ballet, captured with a smooth, steady camera that actually lets you see the action instead of hiding behind chaotic, messy cuts. It is a clear nod to the roots of Asian action cinema, where the environment itself feels alive and any everyday object can instantly become a lethal weapon. The absolute beating heart of the movie is its insane stunt choreography, brought to life by an incredibly dedicated cast. Joe Taslim brings his heavy judo background and a menacing, undeniable charisma that instantly raises the stakes and shifts the weight of every scene he is in. On the flip side, Siam Miao delivers flawless, authentic Shaolin Kung Fu, using his body language to communicate anger and desperation much better than any script could. The fight coordinator, Kensuke Sannomura, did an unbelievable job making the brawls feel painful, exhausting, and real. The fights actually have their own logical rhythm, you see the characters getting tired, feeling the pain, and steadying their opponents to find an opening, which totally makes up for the lack of deep dialogue. However, this non-stop adrenaline rush definitely comes at a cost to the story. The plot is basically just a conveyor belt moving us from one bloody beat down to the next, following the super-cliche formula of a deadly dad trying to rescue his daughter from a crime syndicate. The script is undeniably thin, the dialogue feels stiff, and the villains are basically one-dimensional caricatures with zero psychological depth. There is no real emotional connection or complex rivalry here, the bad guys are just generic mobsters waiting to be thrown into the meat grinder. Plus, you definitely need to suspend your disbelief a bit, as the characters sometimes survive multiple stab wounds and brutal hits as if they were just minor scratches. Surprisingly, though, that extreme simplicity is exactly what saves the film from tripping over itself. By not trying to force a deep, dramatic storyline, the movie never slows down its crazy pace with unnecessary subplots. The basic rescue mission just serves as a straight line giving us an excuse for the on-screen carnage, and the movie fully owns that. The Furious isn't trying to win any awards for screenwriting or revolutionize crime thrillers, and it never pretends otherwise. Instead, it fully embraces its identity as a heavy, straightforward, and flawlessly executed martial arts spectacle that delivers exactly the kind of raw action fans are looking for right up to the very last second.

The_Invite.transcribe: 19th-century Irish novelist, playwright and raconteur Oscar Wilde, widely known for his witticisms and observations about life, is generally credited for the following arguably astute advice, one should always be in love. That is the reason why one should never marry. And it's most fitting that those very words should eloquently serve as a cinematic epigraph at the start of the latest feature from actress-director Olivia Wilde, her best work behind the camera to date. Based on the 2020 Spanish comedy-drama, Sentimental, released domestically as The People Upstairs, this American remake presents an incisive, sometimes brutal, often cynical look at the subject of marriage through the eyes of a long-wedded San Francisco couple, Joe, Seth Rogen, and Angela, Wilde, when they invite their upstairs neighbors, Pina, Penelope Cruz, and Hawk, Edward Norton, to their place for dinner. Admittedly, Joe and Angela don't know their guests well, but they certainly seem to know a lot about them and have developed well-defined opinions about them. The sparks start to fly before Pina and Hawk arrive, however, when it becomes apparent that the hosts are ill-prepared for the festivities, a scenario that reveals much about them and the state of the marriage. And, when the guests arrive, they pick up on the emotional turmoil quickly. Their keen observation skills, in a way, in turn, prompt a series of hilarious, intense and tension-filled episodes with Joe and Angela and, by extension, within each partnership. To say more here would reveal too much, but suffice it to say that the evening is filled with unexpected and provocative twists and turns that leave both couples drastically changed by night's end. Their time together is replete with witty and scathing humor that frequently goes for the jugular, as well as moments of deep drama, heartwarming tenderness and stunning insights about one another. While the film occasionally tries a little too hard to evoke viewer responses, especially at the outset, once the picture finds its groove, it effectively fires on all cylinders, thanks to the outstanding writing and stellar performances of the perfectly cast quartet. The invite feels very much like a Woody Allen movie from the days when he was at the peak without being a blatant copycat. What's more, given that the bulk of the film takes place on one set, it comes across like a play but never feels the least bit stagey, maintaining a steady pace and effectively holding audience attention. This release defied any expectations I might have had about it going into the theatre, a pleasant surprise in itself, but the fact that it shines on so many fronts makes it all the more worthwhile. The picture is admittedly sometimes a little cringy to watch, but it always rebounds, redeeming itself by making you laugh. And that's one invitation I'd always be eager to accept.

You get a sense right from the start that the marriage between Joe, Seth Rogen, and Angela, Olivia Wilde, is running on the fumes of what it once was and that it has been for a while. He returns home from his mundane work as a music teacher to find that she has invited their neighbors for a continental supper. He has no recollection of this having been discussed, but his grump soon has to be restrained when Pina, Penelope Cruz, and Hawk, Edward Norton, arrive. Not unsurprisingly, they quite quickly read the scenario and suggest that this maybe isn't the best time, but Angela insists that they stay and enjoy some jambon and red wine oops, he didn't remember to buy any so they are having to use their secret stash. Rather than settle into a more standard form of polite behavior with their guests, the couple continue to bicker and snap at each other creating the kind of toxic atmosphere you could cut with a cheese knife. All the while, we are also sensing that their guests have a bit of an ulterior motive too, and that becomes altogether clearer when Joe and Pina split from the other pair and what now ensues tests the fabric of their marriage, s. Whilst offering us quite an insightful observation of a couple who are cruising along through life because they can't really be bothered doing anything else. Are they still in love, or even in like? Is their relationship beyond repair or does it just need a kick in the ass? Wilde manages to capture the exasperated wife convincingly and Cruz steals this towards the latter part of this nuptial analysis as her role, that of a counselor, allows her to make some brutally acerbic comments on the state of her host's lives whilst also whipping a few cracks in the direction of her own beau whom Norton plays in an engagingly understated fashion. Never correct a Spaniard's English when she's in full flow. The four actors are all on solid form both together and in their pairings and the comedy, of which there is plenty, comes mostly from writing that is sophisticatedly poignant throughout. Though essentially a critique on human relationships, this also takes a pop at the ridiculousness of faddishness too and the denouement has something quite tales of the unexpected to it, too. It does have something of the theatrical to it and I reckon it would work well on stage. As it is here, though, it's comfortably on par with SESGAY's original short comedy Sentimental, from 2020 and also worth a gander.

The_Last_Sunrise.transcribe: From where I stand, as I have said before, predictability is the cardinal sin of filmmaking. If one can foresee what's going to happen, there's little point in watching the movie, now is there. And, unfortunately, such is the case here in the latest release from director Carlson Young. Based on the best-selling novel of the same name, 2025, by Anna Todd, the cinematic version of this story is a clinic in formulaic filmmaking, where virtually every plot development is apparent from miles away. Indeed, it's the kind of picture better suited to the sappy sensibilities of the hallmarked channel than other less cheesy distribution platforms. The Last Sunrise tells the tale of a young Houston-based dancer, Oriah, aka Rhee, para, Maya Rifico, who's afflicted with a tumorous condition that causes epilepsy. Her prospects aren't favorable after she suffers an on-stage accident, prompting her mother, Isolde Eva Longoria, to take her for a summer's recuperation on the Spanish resort island of Mallorca, where mom is working on a massive new hotel project for a real estate developer. Isolde's also anxious for her daughter to see where her mom grew up and to reconnect to her own roots, but, once there, her work keeps her so busy that she and Rhee spend little time together. With so much free time on her hands, Rhee routinely goes off on her own, a practice that unwittingly takes her to a clothing-optional beach and introduces her to Julian, Fernando Lindes, a bad boy with an attitude who, paradoxically, works as a humble fisherman with a passionate ecological agenda. And, of course, they naturally fall for one another. But, as their holiday romance emerges, they each hide secrets from one another—she, her illness, and he, his outstanding debt to a badass loan shark, all of which are piled atop even bigger disclosures of which neither of them is aware. So how will everything play out? Well, as discussed earlier, that shouldn't be too hard to figure out as all the requisite pieces fall into place neatly on cue. While the narrative shows some improvement as the story progresses, much of it nevertheless follows the standard made-for-TV movie template, with plenty of travelogue-type footage thrown in to exquisitely show off its exotic locale. As for the performances, they represent serious cases of miscasting—Longoria looks bored, tediously walking through her role as if she could have phoned it in. Lindes comes across like a refugee from a designer jeans ad who's desperately in need of English elocution lessons, and Refiko makes for a stunning, vulnerable ingenue, but it's difficult to fathom that she's supposedly as ill as she's said to be, stretching credibility about as tautly as it can go. Fans of romance novels and film versions thereof will undoubtedly find this effort to be right up their alley, but those looking for something with more substance and a lot less frothy fluff can skip this one and not miss a thing.

The_Love_Hypothesis.transcribe: Amazon MGM Studios seems to have found an area where it works pretty well, adapting young adult romances that already come with an established community behind them. The Love Hypothesis is another example. The film, directed by Claire Scanlon, adapts Ollie Hazelwood's novel, which also has a pretty interesting origin, it started out as fan fiction and eventually became a New York Times bestseller. The story follows Olive Smith, Lily Reinhart, a brilliant PhD student who has a much clearer idea of where she wants to take her scientific career than what she wants from her love life. Everything changes after an impulsive kiss leads to a fake relationship with Adam Carlson, Tom Bateman, a professor known for his difficult personality. And from there, the movie knows exactly what it wants to be. What I liked most is that it doesn't try to hide the fact that this is a romance. It doesn't seem embarrassed by its intimate scenes or try to make them completely sanitized just to fit a platform. The movie lets its characters be adults, lets there be genuine attraction between them, and gives that part of their relationship real weight within the story. But above all, it works because of its leads. Lily Reinhart and Tom Bateman have a chemistry that makes the relationship believable. There are moments when you simply buy the fact that these two characters are into each other, and that may sound basic, but in a romance, it's probably one of the most important things. The critical reception has also been pretty positive, with 86% of reviews being favorable on Rotten Tomatoes at the time of writing. I don't think the love hypothesis is reinventing anything. It doesn't need to. It understands exactly what kind of story it wants to tell and, for now, seems pretty comfortable telling it without apologizing for being a romance.

If you're interested in a quick science overview, be see neither the book nor the movie are particularly interested in accurate science, it's extremely common to do gene knockouts in whatever you're testing. The science behind how that happens is kinda complicated and not super important, but really cool, but essentially most lab mice are severely inbred so they have fairly consistent genomes, and then you can take any gene you want to study and turn it off. This is useful for studying the effects of a gene, for example, if you knock out a gene and see that the mice have seven toes, you know it probably has an impact on embryonic development, or you can do it to mimic a disease state so you can test treatment, i.e. you could theoretically knock out the CFTR gene to mimic cystic fibrosis. The movie says Olive knocked out the hanging from a bar gene, which isn't a thing so unsure specifically what she was testing there, but the hanging test is common in mouse studies. I've seen it done in TBI, traumatic brain injury, models where you basically time how long a mouse can hang from a bar. You could be testing strength, muscle coordination, motor skills, or psychological state if you do a tail hang test. So after a TBI, you'd expect loss of motor skills slash coordination so a mouse given a TBI wouldn't hang as long as a healthy mouse. Note that Olive didn't really successfully do this experiment at all on screen. The time when it failed she essentially just threw the mouse on the bar and didn't give it chance to start hanging. So this is real science but not selected very accurately and unsure how it relates to blood biomarkers of pancreatic cancer. The_Mandalorian_and_Grogu.transcribe: Find more reviews at https://www.manualsbento.com rating, be stepping into the theater for The Mandalorian and Grogu. My anticipation was fueled by the undeniable charm of its main duo, and on a purely sensory level, this leap to the big screen absolutely delivers a blockbuster experience worthy of the largest IMAX canvas. From the breathtaking opening set piece, boasting some of the most brutal, intricately choreographed hand-to-hand action in the modern Star Wars mythos, the film immediately sheds the constraints of its streaming origins. Jon Favreau, Iron Man, crafts a visually stunning flick where the production design feels tangible, dirty, and authentic. The tactile delight of practical creature effects blends seamlessly with CGI elements, creating a visually consistent galaxy that disproves any notion of this looking like a glorified TV episode. Elevating this scale is a thunderous revamping of the musical score by Ludwig Garandson, Oppenheimer, which injects an infectious, epic energy into every frame, while the voice work across the board, including stellar additions from Jeremy Allen White, the bear, and Martin Scorsese, Shark Tale, brings an unexpected depth to the ensemble. Yet, as much as my heart swelled seeing Din Djarin remain a magnetic, stoic anchor alongside a fiercely independent, endlessly cute grogu, I cannot shake the feeling that the narrative plays it entirely too safe. The story unfolds in a highly cyclical, repetitive structure, except a mission, face danger, narrowly escape, with jarring transition cuts that practically scream where a TV commercial break or episode boundary should have been. By the time the pacing grinds to a brutal halt in the second half to focus on a quieter, grogucentric sequence, the lack of narrative momentum becomes impossible to ignore. It's a lovely, calm breath of fresh air and isolation, but it exposes a frustrating absence of stakes, a revolving door of half-baked villains, and a status quo that leaves our beloved characters exactly where they started at the end of their last season. It beautifully honours the foundational themes of fatherhood and found family that made us duo, but in refusing to take a genuine narrative risk, it ultimately feels like a spectacular, heartwarming holding pattern. May we always find the courage to venture into unknown territory, for even the most comforting bonds must eventually grow to survive the journey.

Score, 7 out of 10 a hollow return to a beloved galaxy look, I was thrilled to catch up with Din and Grogu. Absolutely thrilled. The reunion we'd all been waiting for. But here's the thing about returning to a place you love, sometimes the magic doesn't quite travel with you. The Mandalorian and Grogu is a case in point. It's not a bad film, not by a long shot. It's just less. Less edge, less grit, less of the spark that made the series so compelling in the first place. And for a movie that essentially is a season 4 of the TV show, compressed into a single cinematic outing, it feels like something is fundamentally missing. The missing edge this is the film's biggest crime. The TV series had a rawness to it, a sense of real stakes and weathered characters operating in a lawless, post-Empire frontier. The movie feels sanded down, more sanitized, somehow hollow. It's not the grit of the series that has been polished away, it's the heart. The characters we loved Din's stoic vulnerability, Grogu's mischievous charm are present, but their connection, the core of the show, feels a little muted. The danger that used to feel palpable now feels orchestrated. Grogu, diminished and underwhelming my biggest personal disappointment was Grogu. He was very underwhelming. His connection to the Force, which was the source of so much wonder and narrative potential in the series, appears to have severely diminished. He's no longer the little powerhouse of chaotic, untamed energy. His participation in the fight scenes was very disappointing. There were moments where you expected him to unleash something, to be the wildcard that saves the day. Instead, he often feels like a passive observer, a cute mascot rather than the force of nature he was becoming. It's a regression that robs the film of its most unique dynamic. The gaps in logic then there are the things that just don't make sense. One moment in particular stood out, when Din and Grogu were overcome with gas in the prison. The Mandalorian helmet allows them to do short stints outside Earth's atmosphere. There is no way the gas should have overwhelmed him. It's the kind of detail that pulls you right out of the experience, a reminder that the internal logic that felt so solid in the show is now being bent to serve a contrived plot point. The cinema of puppetry on a more positive note, I have to commend the film's commitment to practical effects. Many of the creature scenes appear to have been done using practical effects, and some even seen to be composed using stop animation. This is a throwback to a dying art form, and it gives the world a tangible, tactile feel that CGI often can't replicate. It's one area where the film excels, offering a genuine sense of wonder and craftsmanship that feels sorely missing from many modern blockbusters. However, you can't help but wish they'd applied this same level of care to the narrative logic. The verdict bottom line, I did enjoy the movie overall. It's great to see these characters again. But there was definitely disappointment in my mood. It's a 7 out of 10 because the foundation is strong, the performances are solid, and the practical effects work is genuinely charming. It just doesn't ascend to the heights of its predecessor, and the missteps feel more glaring because of it. If you go in expecting a cinematic experience that captures the soul of the show, you might leave feeling like something is missing. Watch if asterisk you're a die-hard fan who just wants to see Din and Grogu on the big screen, and you're willing to accept a diluted version of the magic. Skip if asterisk you want a film that respects the lore and character development of the series. This movie might just leave you feeling short-changed.

The Odyssey belongs to bright Mediterranean sun, blue seas, blue skies, and passionate Hellenic vitality, even amid tragedy. Slapping his Batman-slash-Dunkirk gloom over it makes everything feel oppressive and mismatched, like forcing a Nordic winter onto the Aegean, indeed, he even included Viking-style ships, of course completely unrelated to the period. As one of the 2026 summer movie season's most anticipated releases, writer-director Christopher Nolan's screen adaptation of Homer's literary epic, The Odyssey, has generated more than its share of reactions and for a variety of reasons. So I'll come right to the point on my view of this release, I liked it, but I didn't love it. This retelling of the diverse experiences of Greek warrior Odysseus, Matt Damon, on returning to his Grecian home of Ithaca after fighting in the Trojan War explores the many adventures and profound soul-searching of his 10-year journey, the second half of a 20-year-long absence. Waiting for him back home are his devoted wife, Penelope, and Hathaway, who has long been courted by a band of would-be suitors like Antonis, Robert Pattinson, who believe her husband is dead, and Telemachus, Tom Holland, the son who's never met his father and stands to succeed him as king of Ithaca should he be officially declared deceased. This historic drama, a common reading selection in many high school English lit classes, thus follows the intrigue and adventures from the perspectives of the trip and the home front, many of which viewers are likely to find familiar in this cinematic depiction. However, not everything works in this adaptation. For starters, the film is too long with its 2 hours and 52 minutes runtime, especially during the picture's languishing, talkie opening hour. Then there's the writing, which incorporates more than its share of ill-fitting contemporary dialogue, material that should have never made its way into the final script. And there are noticeable exclusions and underdeveloped sequences from the source material that could have been included and or tweaked in the film narrative with the removal of overlong, extraneous material. For example, despite frequent references to the Greek gods, their presence in the film is largely absent save for a few conversations between Odysseus and Athena, the goddess of wisdom, Zendaya. A similar fate befalls Helen of Troy, Lupita Nyong'o, the woman who launched a thousand ships and prompted the Trojan War in the first place, and Calypso, Charlize Theron, the mysterious caregiver who loves an ailing Odysseus and nurses him back to health for seven years in the midst of his journey. With those shortcomings aside, however, the Odyssey has its share of strengths, too, such as the picture's decidedly engaging second half, as well as its fine performances, especially those of Hathaway, Pattinson, Holland and Samantha Morton as Circe, a witch whom Odysseus encounters during the trip home. Those looking for action-adventure segments will find plenty of those here as well, although the special effects depicting them are noticeably inconsistent, great in sequences like the Greeks' ambush of their opponents' stronghold with the ploy of the Trojan horse and the soldiers' dangerous encounter with the massive, menacing whirlpool Charybdis, and not-so-great during their contacts with the seductively voiced Sirens, the one-eyed giant Cyclops and the multi-headed, cliff-dwelling monster Scylla. It's difficult to pinpoint exactly how and why this production failed to live up to some of the high expectations that had been set for it, though it's a safe bet that it might have fallen prey to believing its own pre-release hype, especially coming off of the impressive and well-earned success of Nolan's previous effort, Oppenheimer, 2023. Obviously, viewers will have to make up their own minds, but keeping the foregoing impressions in mind may prove helpful in formulating those opinions as audiences wend their way through their own personal odysseys.

With a production design worthy of Sir Ridley Scott, Christopher Nolan takes us into antiquity for his take on the second installment of Homer's Trojan War Stories. I have to say it's maybe not the most impressive of wooden horses that is left as a tribute for the maybe just a little too gullible Trojans, but now we know that this decade-long siege has all ended in a mighty conflagration and that Odysseus, Matt Damon, is keen on returning to Ithaca where his wife and son await him. On that island though, strife is rife. Penelope and Hathaway is being besieged by an army of suitors like Antinous, Robert Pattinson, and the young Telemachus, Tom Holland, isn't really best equipped to step in and protect his mother from their machinations. Now flitting between the island's domestic issues and the legendary trials of the returning husband, Nolan tries to weave the two threads together in quite a compelling fashion. The snag for me throughout this epic drama is that we spent too much time on Ithaca with the family issues and not enough time with Odysseus and his crew as they faced a plethora of deadly foes and evil temptations as they traversed the Mediterranean. Too many of their adventures are too tightly compressed and involve a few scenes of menace before everyone rushes back to their ships, usually fewer than arrived, before continuing on their dangerous travels. Much is told thanks to his memory-provoking conversation with the lotus-peddling calypso, Charlize Theron, but again, we don't really get to grips much with who she is or what he is doing on her beautiful island. Charybdis and the sirens, even the Cyclops are all given a little too much short shrift as we dwell more at the other end of his voyage on the issues facing the young Telemachus as he travels to Sparta to find news from Menelaus and his now-restored wife Helen. The visual effects are pretty spectacular and Damon manages quite well to craft a character who is brave and ingenious but also troubled by both the destruction of Troy and by his behaviour whilst participating in that. What we also avoid here is much involvement from the Olympians. Barring some regular references to Zeus's laws of hospitality and a few scenes with Athena, Zendaya, who appears to be acting more as his psychiatrist than a goddess of war and wisdom whose statue was unceremoniously decapitated during the assault of the city and whose temple was unceremoniously defiled, we don't really involve them. If you've read even the briefest of adaptations of the novel, you'll know that many of his difficulties getting home were due to the anger of gods like Poseidon and Apollo, yet those characters remain somewhat omnipresent. Perhaps, and I don't write this lightly, three hours simply isn't long enough to do justice to the characterful complexities of the story. I did enjoy this and it flew past, but I really wanted much more of the fantastic, the horror and the terror and maybe just a little less of the troubled souls presented here, and I was just a little bit disappointed as I left. Perhaps he's saving more for the director's cut?

Score, 2 out of 10 an epic that lost its way home what did I miss? That's the question I kept asking myself throughout Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. I was expecting so much more. The pedigree was undeniable, Nolan behind the camera, a staggering ensemble cast, a legendary source material that has endured for nearly three millennia. And yet, what unfolded on screen was, to put it bluntly, like watching a kid's movie. The tone problem, a myth for children Homer's Odyssey is not a children's story. It is a brutal, bloody, morally complex epic about a man who survives a decade of war only to spend another decade fighting monsters, gods, and his own flaws to get home. It deals with temptation, infidelity, vengeance, and the sheer, grinding cost of survival. Nolan's film, however, feels sanitized. The violence is bloodless. The monsters are cartoonish. The gods are reduced to plot devices. The moral ambiguities that make Odysseus a fascinating, flawed hero are sanded down into a bland, heroic archetype. This is a film that seems terrified of its own darkness. It wants the prestige of Homer without the discomfort. The Coen brothers did it better and here's the thing that kept nagging at me throughout, The Coen brothers did so much more with the material in Oh Brother, where Art Thou, their 2000 film is a loose, depression-era adaptation of the Odyssey, and it crackles with wit, heart, and genuine thematic depth. It understands that the power of Homer's epic lies not in the monsters or the spectacle, but in the characters their flaws, their longings, their stubborn, flawed humanity. The Coens took the bones of the story and built something alive, something that resonated with audiences who had never read a line of Homer. Nolan, by contrast, has taken the same bones and dressed them in expensive but lifeless armor. Oh Brother is a classic that grows richer with every viewing. This Odyssey will be forgotten before the year is out. The performances, wasted talent the cast is extraordinary on paper. But extraordinary actors cannot save underwritten roles. The supporting players, and there are many are given little more than extended cameos. They appear, deliver exposition, and vanish. There is no time to develop relationships, no room for chemistry to breathe. The emotional beats that should land with devastating force the reunion with Penelope, the recognition by Argos, the slaughter of the suitors pass by with a shrug. The visuals, spectacle without soul Nolan is a master of practical effects and large format cinematography, and there are moments of genuine visual grandeur. But spectacle without emotional investment is just noise. The set pieces feel disconnected, more like theme park attractions than narrative climaxes. The Cyclops is impressive in scale but lacks menace. The Sirens are beautiful but forgettable. The sea journeys that should feel epic feel episodic. The pacing, a slog and a rush the film cannot decide what it wants to be. It rushes through key moments Odysseus's time with Calypso, the encounter with Circe while lingering on others that add little. The result is a film that feels both overstuffed and underdeveloped. It is, at times, genuinely boring. The verdict The Odyssey is a profound disappointment. It takes one of the greatest stories ever told and reduces it to a shallow, sanitized, emotionally hollow spectacle. It is a kids movie version of a myth that was never meant for children. It earns its 2 out of 10 for the undeniable craft on display and the occasional glimpse of what could have been. But craft without soul is just a hollow shell. Watch if asterisk you want a visually polished but emotionally empty introduction to the story or you're a completist for Nolan's filmography. Skip if asterisk you love Homer, you love epic storytelling, or you expect a film worthy of its source. This is not it. The Coen brothers did it better with a fraction of the budget and a tenth of the self-importance.

Took me a full two months to get around to seeing this, and I credit CD's opinion with influencing that choice. I went to IMAX and the cinema was packed, felt like a real event near an opening night. I felt meh too after coming out. It wasn't bad. It was an interpretation of the story, with good cinematography, ridiculously overpowering sound. It didn't seem unfaithful to the details of the story to me, just the tone. I read it again this year and yes, it was not a story about one man's PTSD from the sack of Troy. It was about his epic journey home, suffering on the way, and the faithfulness of his family and court who were left behind against faithless adversity. The drawn-out recapture of Ithaca is much like the timing of the book, but the final payoff when he reunites with Penelope in the book is much bigger. It's a fair cop by CD that Odysseus doesn't seem that invested in getting home at all, and definitely a fair cop that the dialogue sucked and the acting that it then forced onto an ensemble cast of fantastic actors was underwhelming. My sister was with us and said afterwards I didn't really appreciate what an anti-war message was in this story and I had to say, well I think that's dramatic license. Which brings us back to what is permissible in that. Homer may not have even been an actual person, this was mythology handed down over centuries, through a dark age for ancient Greece. A story full of hyperbole, intended probably to entertain and instruct children. Almost certainly never told in a single sitting. Written by Greeks about a people from a previous time, so already appropriative even then. What did ancient Greeks really know about 12th century people who lived in the same region? Archaeology wasn't a thing, history itself wasn't. This was it, as far as instruction in history went, along with already garbling stories about more recent events told by elders, dressed up to make them sound better. And the story continues to adapt, despite being fixed and written verse eventually and being called the work of Homer. The verse gets adapted as the language changes and the stories are retold. Virgil adapts the fall of Troy to slip an incidental character out of the sack of Troy to become an insanely important character in Roman history, the founder of Rome. He slips people of his time into the story, because he is determined to flatter Augustus, his patron. And on it goes. The work is translated into many languages. It is retold in different ways, I was well familiar with much of Homer from reading children's books as a kid, just as I was familiar with the tale of King Arthur despite not reading Mallory or any older sources. In all of these children's retellings, though, there was an attempt to carry through the spirit of the original, that the characters were heroic, even if flawed. We were meant to actually like them. Perhaps that is an affectation of the late 20th century, in the traditions of a fading empire, the British, during the wild heyday of a triumphant one, the USA, in which we are all looking for heroes as little boys and cowboy movies will suffice if you happen to come from somewhere cowboys were a thing once, and you happen to be a boy. For me it was Star Wars, which has cowboys and evil English Empire people. Girls can read whatever they want too, there's no real shortage. Then we get a convergence of cinematic events into grand epic retellings aimed at an audience from literally everywhere, and have to tell the story so everyone feels included, or consciously choose not to, or some blend of both. This was a blend, of course, that's the entire history of this story. An artist is entirely permitted to do whatever they like with this one. I am, however, not forced to enjoy it. In the end I was browbeaten into seeing it, because my son wanted to, some of his mates said it was awesome, my wife thought I should see it in the cinema because I'm a classics lover, my mother thought it was great and thoroughly recommended IMAX, and my sister expressed an interest so long as someone else paid for the tickets, which my wife did without really asking me, and so there it is, I spend a cold Sunday night catching a train to a city IMAX because you can't just park on the street outside the theater the way we did when I was a kid. It was a whole thing, car, walk, train, walk, watch, walk who bus, walk, car, by time I got back home to do what I would have chosen to do of a Sunday evening. It felt like a mini-odyssey of my own. All of the sense of occasion about it inspires me to write a long comment about a review about a movie about an adaption of a collection of adapted stories, about events that most likely didn't happen to somebody who probably did exist. I decided not to be a sad old C-word who begrudged the $200 the whole experience cost in Auckland, and to stay moderately positive to my family about it rather than make them feel guilty for wanting to be entertained and experience cultural touchstones of the time. I save my true feelings for you, dear reader, that guy slash gal out there who got this far. It was okay. I've seen worse and better. How do you rate something when you've seen thousands of movies, hundreds of them great? Did it get into the top 200? Probably not for me, I reserve that for movies where I feel like I would want to watch it again, and I didn't feel it. I can understand that people who are less jaded by five decades of amazing cinema could feel differently, feel a bit more attached to the characters. Spider-Man was at least trying in this movie, I liked him a little bit. At least he cried when his daddy came home and his old doggy died with joy at seeing him again. Perhaps I am like Odysseus myself, emotionally incapable of feeling a strong response to the spectacle. That might be how it looks from the outside. Perhaps that was what I didn't like about the movie, that it depicts an old man, Odysseus at the end and me are probably the same age as an emotional cripple, but I don't have some epic tale of suffering to justify it, just an epic tale of suffering so many entertainment events that in the end I just wanted to get home and go to bed. Is this the tale of my time? If it is, it could even be a true depiction, but it's not something I would recommend to others, at least not without first seeing the other 500 movies I liked more. But hell, on Netflix it's only costing you like 50 C, so maybe watch it then if everyone's talking about it. Or go to the cinema and form your own opinions, gets you out of the house I suppose.

The_Runner.transcribe: Pulse-pounding deadline-based thrillers have become a common source of action-adventure viewing over the years. These largely formulaic offerings are often fairly predictable, with their outcomes frequently obvious well in advance, the only variable generally being the routes their narratives take to arrive at their final destinations. So it is again with this latest effort from director Kevin MacDonald, a typically capable filmmaker who comes up woefully short with this release. When London-based criminal attorney Maya Martin, Gal Gadot, goes on her usual morning run before her latest big court case, she's interrupted in mid-sprint by a cell phone call, supposedly from her young son, Noah, Rory Wilmot. However, when she answers, she discovers it's not from him but, instead, from an anonymous mystery caller, Damian Lewis, who has kidnapped Noah and threatens she follows his instructions to the letter. Specifically, the kidnapper wants Maya to murder a key witness in the case against his former employer, a high-profile mobster accused of killing two young women. But, to ensure that she complies with his directives, the caller says he's tracking her movements by tapping into the geolocator on her cell phone. This requires her to remain out in the open, on the street, a plan that calls for the former champion pentathlete to run five miles across London in an hour to the hotel where the witness is in protective custody prior to his transfer to the courthouse. This setup thus launches the protagonist into retrek across the city, a journey filled with twists, turns, thrills, spills and the revelation of a variety of highly personal details, including long-held secrets. But is she up to this task? You get three guesses. As this scenario unfolds, though, the story is peppered with an array of credibility-stretching implausibilities that not even Wonder Woman herself is realistically capable of pulling off. Indeed, while tales like this typically call for viewers to suspend belief, many of the developments in this plot-hole-ridden story are just plain difficult to accept. Admittedly, the narrative is stylishly dressed up in a superbly edited, fast-paced package with some inventive cinematography that shows off street-level London exquisitely, but such window dressing still can't conceal the plethoric flaws in the script. With better writing and plot scrutiny, the runner might have made for some late-summer escapist fun, but it's hard to fathom it as being much more than a paycheck for the principles involved and yet another in an ongoing string of substandard outings for Amazon Studios.

You've seen this film before. When it was 1995's Nick of Time and Die Hard with a Vengeance, 2002's Phonebooth, 2003's Out of Time, 2005's Red Eye, or even Netflix's Carry On, 2024, well, you get the idea. Films like The Runner do not happen in a vacuum. And the formula is clearly working, as director Kevin MacDonald's film, wisely released direct to streaming on Amazon Prime, is already one of the platform's top films. Starring Gal Gadot as high-powered London barrister Maya, whose child is held for ransom by a mysterious caller, Damian Lewis. In exchange for assassinating the star witness of a local mob trial, it's a premise that sounds increasingly preposterous the more you think about it. Despite its run-lola-run pacing, with endless clips of Gal Gadot sprinting across every tourist locale in London, from St Paul's to Canary Wharf, the implausibility of running the London marathon in 84 minutes strains credulity. The always one-step-ahead omniscience of Lewis's character, effortlessly bending hacked technology to his whims, is another worn-out trope that refuses to die. As diabolical and meticulous as Lewis is, one wonders why he doesn't just carry out the assassination himself instead of putting Gadot through a series of ridiculous time trials during the hustle and bustle of midday London. And while Gadot gamely carries the physical desperation of a single mother trying to save her child, unfortunately, the film leans into her limited range as an actress, with dull dialogue and pointless conversational exposition. As a tense action thriller, The Runner will probably appeal to anyone unfamiliar with any of the aforementioned films in this subgenre. But for anyone else, this is a paint-by-numbers slog through familiar terrain that will do nothing for Gadot's post-**wonderwoman**career.

For those who grew up with these characters, it's impossible to remain indifferent to the magic emanating from every animated frame or the way this space odyssey manages to transform nostalgia into something vibrant and new. Now I know that I'm not really the demographic for this, but I didn't mind the last one from 2023 so had an open mind as it started. Princess Peach is kidnapped by the menacing baby bowser who is none too pleased that his dad has been locked up. He is determined to use her as leverage to free him, but that is exactly what intrepid and ingenious Mario and Luigi intend to thwart. What now ensues is the thinnest of stories stretched across a messy collection of interstellar scenarios as they bounce from world to world trying to rescue the royal damsel in distress. I always reckoned that the amiable mushroom people belonged more in an Arabian Nights tale than a sci-fi cartoon, but even their innocent cheeriness can't really enliven this rapidly and colorfully edited together sequence of pinball machine style scenes. There is surprisingly little effort made to characterize either the goodies or the baddies, and the frenetic nature of the animation barely leaves us time to draw breath before we ascend to another level and pretty much repeat as before, only with slightly different props and goals. It's not so much that this lacks a beginning, middle and end, it is more that it just comes across as content sequence of scenes that could all see the film conclude as predictably as the sun coming up. Perhaps very young children might enjoy the sheer buzz of this, but there really isn't anything visually or from the script to entertain the grown-ups. I bet the merch merchants are happy, though.

You know how, sometimes, you get a burger that's so thin, overcooked, and leathery that it stops being a burger and starts being a vehicle for condiments? That, to me, is Super Mario Galaxy. The story slash writing is simply there to deliver Nintendo brand nostalgia. As someone with deep love and fond memories of Nintendo, I'm okay with this but I'm not going to pretend that the story is the narrative equivalent of Wagyu Beef. Contrary to what some of the less charitable critics say, the movie does have a cogent story. Bowser Jr. aims to rescue his father from his imprisonment and bring the dreams they shared when Junior was young to fruition. To do that, he kidnaps Princess Rosalina, the mother of the stars, to siphon her magic. The gang sets off to rescue the princess. A simple enough premise, certainly serviceable. It isn't winning any awards for novelty but not everything needs to be high art to be enjoyable. But it fails on even this modest ambition. The execution is riddled with enough underscore Deus Ex underscore to fill a Greek pantheon. Character motivations are inconsistent without real evolution. There are so many zany little subplots that it's like they worried that the audience's attention span would run out yet they still made the thing run for over two hours. Fortunately, the metaphorical condiment was delicious like biting into that burger expecting Hunt's ketchup but getting homemade garlic aioli mayo. The quality of the animation made the film's many callbacks enjoyable. I found myself smiling a lot and actually thinking dang, I really underscore should underscore get around to playing, redacted Mario games. Which, I'm certain is all Nintendo really hoped for rather than making a genuinely excellent standalone cinematic experience. In sum, it's not something I regret seeing especially with my family. Though it is something I wish I had saved the video games worth of money waiting for it to come out on streaming rather than seeing it in theaters.

I would recommend watching if you've seen the first and if you've played Mario Galaxy.

Director James Ashcroft's The Whisper Man is a hodgepodge of other suspense thrillers you've already seen. Sometimes it's the silence of the lambs, then Blackphone, or the lesser-seen Sean Penn's The Pledge, 2001. With one of the most enviable casts in recent memory, the story takes place in the soggy, dark suburbs of New Jersey, where widower and single father Tom Kennedy, Adam Scott, moves into a new home with his socially awkward son, Jake. And with Hocum earlier this year isn't Scott tired of playing novelists? Estranged from his decorated, long-retired detective father Peter Willis, Robert De Niro, Tom's already complicated life becomes considerably worse when an old, and solved, serial killer case appears to have produced a copycat killer, as the bodies of small children begin turning up again. Local detective Amanda Beck, Michelle Monahan, enlists Willis's help in trying to uncover clues, just as Tom's son suddenly goes missing. Co-starring Hamish Linklater, Michael Keaton, and Owen Teague who each arguably upstage De Niro, Scott and Monahan hear the plot eventually congeals into a rote and rather predictable conclusion that will unfortunately result in being almost instantly forgettable. With two Oscar winners, capable performances by Scott and Monahan, and directing by New Zealand's Ashcroft, who stunned in 2021 with Coming Home in the Dark, The Whisper Man struggles to pick a lane, vacillating between being a supernatural thriller, a detective story, and a serial killer film. It is this indecision that appears to hurt the film most as, again, the performances from the supporting cast save the film from being a total waste of time.

The Wrecking Crew is aptly named. This action flick, for me, early on wrecked any chance that I'd actually enjoy this film. I'll put my hand up and say I'm sick and tired of the gratuitous violence oozing out of Hollywood. The light, jokey tone of this film is at odds with oftentimes really ugly violence. Entirely smashing someone's upper teeth against a table in the opening scenes is one such example. It's not funny, it's not okay, it's not entertaining, no matter who it's done to. Regrettably, given how violent US society is, perhaps I should not be surprised, but it's also one of the reasons I don't watch a great deal of US cinema these days. Beyond that, the actions of the formulaic variety and the bro-buddy backstory has long since ossified into a cliché. In summary, tone it down, Hollywood. Excessive violence is not okay. If you want to make a light-toned action flick, then try doing just that.

Tom_Clancy's_Jack_Ryan_Ghost_War.transcribe: Watchable, but the underlying message isn't a good one. That's my core takeaway from Jack Ryan, Ghost War. Yes, by all means, watch this film as a basic, wholly familiar and predictable but nonetheless enjoyable action romp. Expect decent pacing, lots of action and mildly engaging characters. All that said, pushing the belief that doing horrible things to people is somehow redeemable in order to keep the world safe isn't good on any level. As we are seeing, the US's belief in its primacy has led to countless deaths and seemingly endless wars. In summary, quite watchable when viewed as a formulaic action flick, but the message it's trying to push is an ugly one, absent a solid moral grounding.

Tony.transcribe: Stories about challenged individuals who managed to turn their lives around are immensely popular with moviegoing audiences. But there's a big difference between those that depict individuals who beat the odds against them and those featuring characters who have to dig themselves out of their own self-created holes, and it should be easy to guess which ones are more well-liked. Such latter circumstances are the ones in play in this biographical comedy-drama from writer-director Matt Johnson, an origin story about how celebrity chef and culinary travelogue host Anthony Bourdain, 1956-2018, got his start. In 1975, Bourdain, who curtly and routinely informed others that he simply wanted to be called Tony, Dominic Cessa, was enrolled at Vassar College in one of the first classes to which men had been admitted to the former all-women's institution. He was seeking, with brazenly conceded confidence and no credible experience, a writing fellowship that would allow him avoid going home for the summer, a prospect he viewed with palpable disdain. However, when he was turned down for the opportunity, he needed to find a different path. He decided to head to the coastal resort town of Provincetown, Massachusetts to pursue his romantic interest, or, more accurately, romantic obsession, from high school, currently a Vassar co-ed, Nancy Pukoski, Amelia Jones, who was spending the summer on Cape Cod. Tony told others that he was making the journey to work on the fellowship he didn't win as a cover for his pursuit of a relationship with someone who typically responded to his advances with ambivalence. These conditions ostensibly forced him to wing it in every conceivable way upon arrival in P-town. And, as fate would have it, the aspiring writer was the same loudish narcissist there that he was beforehand. After a series of questionable misadventures, he sheepishly ended up taking a job as a dishwasher in a restaurant run by a demanding taskmaster chef, Antonio Banderas, staffed by an array of colourful co-workers, Leo Woodall, Stavros Halkias, who were anything but positive influences. But, as Tony's summer unfolded, he unwittingly began turning things around, largely thanks to the chef's stringent tutelage, launching Tony down another new path that would lead him to a storied future. Bourdain's subsequent success is not depicted here except in the film's electronic epilogue, but it's that implication that arguably grants this story its salvation in light of how it starts out. The protagonist is clearly depicted as an admittedly charismatic, though undeniably uncouth, bad boy who probably wouldn't have otherwise been cut any slack were it not for his accomplishments later in life. Fittingly, Sessa capably makes the most of that characterisation, turning in a badass portrayal and a remarkably on-point impersonation of the title character, even if it's written rather monodimensionally and delivered through an uncannily familiar performance to the actor's role in The Holdovers, 2023, which, unavoidably, raises potential questions about typecasting. It also doesn't help that Tony's backstory is largely missing, with virtually no explanation behind his motivations, behaviour and attitude at this time of his life other than through an epigraphic quote from Bourdain at the film's outset. And this oversight, for what it's worth, may leave viewers wondering why they should care about what happens to him. Those considerations aside, though, the picture has definite strengths of note, particularly the impressive supporting cast of Banderas, Woodall and Halkias, who do much to bolster viewer interest in the narrative. The film's superb period piece production design and fine cinematography also add much to the picture, particularly the character of this release's time frame. Overall, though, Tony feels as though it could have been stronger, better focused and more engaging. It's modestly entertaining, but, in coming away from it, I felt as though I was only served appetisers and missed out on the main course.

I reckon Anthony Bourdain has a lot to be thankful to a girl called Nancy Foer, for without her inspiration and his hormones, he might never have gone to Providence in 1975 and discovered how to shuck an oyster. Serendipity is fairly omnipresent for him so he bumps into her amongst the thousands of seasonal tourists only to find that she is already working in a pizza place for the summer and has a bow. Tony decides to drown his sorrows and being a bit of a lightweight on that front we find that Six Beers appears to do the trick before he is tossed out onto the street and duly robbed. Luckily, the owner of the flagship from whence he was evicted, Antonio Banderas, takes pity on this poor waif and offers him a job as a dishwasher in his kitchen. His is an eclectic staff with Sal, Leo Woodall, leading a fairly disparate group of skivvies churning out the same four dishes day in, day out. He still hasn't give up on his Nancy, Amelia Jones, though and so for the next while we watch as just about everyone comes to terms with the fact that he's a fairly pathological liar who also happens to have a decent character underneath this constantly evolving facade. As biopics go, Matt Johnson and Cessa have crafted something really quite engagingly plausible here. They are not afraid to cast Bourdain as a bit of a selfish prat who is just as much difficulty owning up to himself who he is as he has to the others whom he is constantly trying to impress. His characterization is one that is only just on the right side of the rails some of the time and his association with Sal, a bad influence rather too convincingly portrayed by Woodall, serves as a counterbalance to the more stabilizing effect provided by an understated Banderas whose chef clearly has a story of his own to tell. There's fun to be had here, too, with a little bit of derision of the pomposity of youthful academic aspirations and of the introspectin that can imbue in a man and there are plenty of buckets of water thrown on his thankfully extensive collection of brightly colored waif fronts. It also reminds us of the declining appreciation of community and if you've ever wondered how to organize a charity clam bake then this is your film. Thanks to Banderas, it's touching at times, usually quite entertaining and well worth a look.
